title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
6. Probabilities, residuals and uncertainty
The fitted outputs are \(\hat\pi=\operatorname{sigmoid}(X\hat\beta)\), not labels obtained by a 0.5 threshold. Response residuals are \(y-\hat\pi\). For conventional maximum-likelihood inference,
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat W X)^{-1},
\qquad \operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}}.\]
Information is recalculated at the final estimate. There is no multiplication by \(\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p)\). Large-sample Wald inference uses
\[z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j,\qquad
p_j=2P(Z\ge|z_j|),\qquad
\operatorname{CI}_{95\%,j}=\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\,\operatorname{SE}_j.\]
Here \(Z\) is standard normal: these are asymptotic z-tests, not the exact Gaussian t-tests used for OLS. Sparse outcomes or near-separation can make Wald inference unreliable even if a finite fit exists. Coefficient intervals are on the log-odds scale; exponentiating their endpoints gives Wald intervals for odds ratios.

eta = X @ beta
fitted = expit(eta)
residuals = y-fitted
exponential = np.exp(-np.abs(eta))
root_weights = np.sqrt(exponential)/(1+exponential)
_, singular_values, Vt = np.linalg.svd(root_weights[:,None]*A,full_matrices=False)
inverse = (Vt.T/singular_values) @ (Vt/singular_values[:,None])
covariance = inverse/scales[:,None]/scales[None,:]
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
z_statistics = beta/se
p_values = 2*norm.sf(np.abs(z_statistics))
conf_int = np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])
show_matrix(r"\hat\pi",fitted)
show_matrix(r"\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)",covariance)
show_matrix(r"X^\top(y-\hat\pi)",X.T @ residuals)
show_dot(r"\hat\eta_1",X[0],beta)
display(pd.DataFrame({"estimate":beta,"SE":se,"z":z_statistics,"p":p_values,
                      "lower 95%":conf_int[:,0],"upper 95%":conf_int[:,1],"odds ratio":np.exp(beta)},
                     index=["intercept","study_hours","practice_score"]))
display(pd.DataFrame({"observed":y,"probability":fitted,"response residual":residuals}).head(8))

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
7. Likelihood, deviance and AIC
For individual binary observations, the saturated model fits every outcome with probability 0 or 1 and has limiting log-likelihood zero. Thus
\[D=-2\ell(\hat\beta),\qquad \mathrm{AIC}=2p-2\ell(\hat\beta).\]
With an explicit ones column, the null model estimates a constant probability \(\bar y\). Without that column, our null convention has no coefficients and fixed probability 0.5. null_deviance is minus twice that null log-likelihood. df_residual is \(n-p\), but it is not used to estimate a Bernoulli dispersion or select a t distribution. The result intentionally has no OLS R-squared or sigma.

ll = log_likelihood(beta)
null_ll = np.sum(y*np.log(y.mean())+(1-y)*np.log1p(-y.mean()))
calculated = dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z_statistics,
                  p_values=p_values,conf_int=conf_int,fitted=fitted,residuals=residuals,
                  log_likelihood=ll,deviance=-2*ll,null_deviance=-2*null_ll,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)
print({key:calculated[key] for key in ["log_likelihood","deviance","null_deviance","aic","df_residual"]})

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
section: 8. Separation, assumptions and things to try
text:
8. Separation, assumptions and things to try
If a predictor combination puts every success on one side and every failure on the other, coefficients can grow without bound while likelihood improves. This is complete separation: there is no finite unpenalized MLE. Quasi-complete separation allows some observations on the boundary. The implementation checks whether an encountered coefficient vector certifies separation; it also rejects rank-deficient information and iteration exhaustion. It is not an exhaustive linear-programming separation detector and does not guarantee detection of every numerically difficult case. It never returns a converged: false partial fit.
The fit requires both classes, finite full-rank inputs, and \(n>p\). This walkthrough uses individual 0/1 outcomes. phit also accepts prior weights, grouped-binomial proportions with trial weights, and offsets (see Matrix model functions). It offers no penalties, Firth correction, or automatic threshold selection. The model assumes independent observations and linear log-odds in the supplied predictors. Missing-data deletion occurs before estimation and warns as in OLS; see the contract.
Try predicting the result before changing the notebook: set all outcomes to 1; replace the outcome by study_hours > 6; duplicate a predictor; convert hours to minutes; or remove the ones column. Which change causes an error, changes the meaning of a coefficient, or changes the null model? Comparing these cases is a way to connect estimation, identifiability and units.

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
Rust connections
fit_logistic takes ownership of Vec<Vec<f64>> and Vec<f64>, then converts them into nalgebra’s dynamic DMatrix and DVector. The matrix constructor explicitly reads the supplied row order; nalgebra stores its matrix internally by columns. Expressions such as &scaled * &candidate borrow those matrices for an operation so subsequent iterations can reuse them. Iterators build weights, score residuals and output vectors without PHP types entering the core.
LogisticResult is a struct holding the complete fit. Result<LogisticResult, StatsError> makes unsuccessful estimation explicit; the ? operator propagates failed decomposition or line-search operations. There is no mutable model object or general optimizer interface. The dedicated loop updates trial coefficients, checks progress, then recomputes information at the accepted final coefficients.
The binding validates PHP integer/float values, removes missing rows according to policy, calls this owned Rust function, and inserts its vectors and scalars into a PHP associative array. Core errors become PHP exceptions, and deletion produces a warning with row metadata. See the OLS Rust learning notes for more explanation of the shared language constructs.
Sources: R glm, R summary.glm, separation and finite estimates.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text: The random-intercept walkthrough introduces clustering. Here we allow each subject both a different starting reaction time and a different response to days of sleep deprivation, using the published sleepstudy data. The optimizer audit verifies this model against R lme4 and statsmodels under ML and REML.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Observations and matrices
\[
y_i=o_i+x_i^\top\beta+z_i^\top b_{g(i)}+\epsilon_i,
\qquad b_g\sim N(0,\Sigma),\quad
\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2/w_i).
\]
Here o is a known offset, w is a positive prior weight, x contains fixed predictors and z contains random predictors. For sleepstudy, o=0, w=1 and both local designs have [1, Days] columns. The ones construct an intercept; Days is observed data. Beta contains the population intercept and slope. Each group’s b contains deviations from those population coefficients, not a second set of observed predictors.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Covariance through a Cholesky factor
Instead of optimizing variance/correlation entries directly, optimize a lower triangular relative factor:
\[
L=\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\c&d\end{bmatrix},\qquad a,d\geq0,
\qquad\Sigma=\sigma^2LL^\top
=\sigma^2\begin{bmatrix}a^2&ac\\ac&c^2+d^2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This guarantees positive semidefinite covariance, including valid zero-variance or perfect-correlation boundaries. A negative c can represent negative intercept/slope covariance. lme4’s lower-triangle parameter ordering is column-major: [a, c, d]. Several terms concatenate their parameters in supplied term order.

from scipy.linalg import cholesky
reference=c['references']['bobyqa']['result']
Sigma=np.array(reference['terms'][0]['covariance'])
sigma2=reference['residual_variance'];L=cholesky(Sigma/sigma2,lower=True)
matrix_tex(L,'L');matrix_tex(sigma2*L@L.T,r'\widehat\Sigma')
print('Intercept SD (ms):',np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]))
print('Slope SD (ms/day):',np.sqrt(Sigma[1,1]))
print('Intercept/slope correlation:',Sigma[0,1]/np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]*Sigma[1,1]))

These are estimates from the full sample. The off-diagonal dot product a*c + 0*d produces the covariance after multiplying by sigma². Variances have different physical units because the second coefficient is measured in milliseconds per day.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: Penalized least squares profiles out beta and random effects
text:
Penalized least squares profiles out beta and random effects
Repeat L once per group to construct block-diagonal Lambda. Write b=Lambda u, where u has spherical covariance sigma²I. Given theta, minimize
\[
q(\theta)=\min_{u,\beta}
\left\|W^{1/2}(y-o-X\beta-Z\Lambda u)\right\|^2+\|u\|^2.
\]
The first term fits observed reaction times; the second penalizes implausibly large standardized random effects. This is a consequence of their Gaussian likelihood, not an arbitrary regularization parameter chosen by the user. It is the least-squares problem
\[
\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}Z\Lambda&W^{1/2}X\\I&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}u\\\beta\end{bmatrix}
\approx\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}(y-o)\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For a selected theta, linear algebra finds u and beta. The nonlinear optimizer searches theta only. We solve with QR; coefficients do not come from explicitly inverting a normal-equation matrix.

from scipy.linalg import block_diag,solve_triangular
Lambda=block_diag(*([L]*len(order)))
A=np.block([[Z@Lambda,x],[np.eye(Z.shape[1]),np.zeros((Z.shape[1],x.shape[1]))]])
b=np.r_[y,np.zeros(Z.shape[1])]
Q,R=np.linalg.qr(A,mode='reduced');solution=solve_triangular(R,Q.T@b)
u=solution[:Z.shape[1]];beta=solution[Z.shape[1]:];effects=Lambda@u
residual=y-x@beta-Z@effects
q=residual@residual+u@u
print('Augmented design:',A.shape)
print('beta:',beta)
print('Observation residual contribution:',residual@residual)
print('Random-effect penalty contribution:',u@u)
print('Total profiled q:',q)
assert np.allclose(beta,reference['coefficients'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)
assert np.allclose(effects.reshape(-1,2),reference['terms'][0]['effects'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)

beta: [251.40510485  10.46728596]
Observation residual contribution: 98881.64284605399
Random-effect penalty contribution: 17697.86289393207

The code uses an additional QR compression before optimization. QR of weighted [Z, X/scales, y-offset] preserves every trial residual norm. Each trial needs only that compact square-root summary plus identity penalty rows. This extends the earlier cached random-intercept idea. The current general summary is dense; lme4 uses sparse factorization to support larger random designs.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: ML and REML are different objectives
text:
ML and REML are different objectives
With C=W⁻¹+Z Lambda Lambdaᵀ Zᵀ, the profiled Gaussian ML scale is
\[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=q/n.\]
The negative profiled marginal log-likelihood is
\[
-\ell_{ML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
n\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/n)\}+\log|C|
\right].
\]
REML adjusts for estimating the p fixed coefficients. It uses
\[
\hat\sigma^2_{REML}=q/(n-p),
\]
and the restricted criterion
\[
-\ell_{REML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
(n-p)\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/(n-p))\}
+\log|C|+\log|X^\top C^{-1}X|
\right].
\]
REML changes the optimization objective, not merely the final denominator. Its extra determinant accounts for fixed-effect estimation. Both determinants come from triangular QR factors in our implementation. Scaling fixed columns requires restoring their determinant contribution, even though scaling does not change the fitted mean. REML likelihood values should not compare different fixed-effect designs.

qr_random=R[:Z.shape[1],:Z.shape[1]]
qr_fixed=R[Z.shape[1]:,Z.shape[1]:]
logdet_C=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_random))).sum()
logdet_info=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_fixed))).sum()
df=len(y)-x.shape[1]
reml_variance=q/df
reml_ll=-.5*(df*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1+np.log(reml_variance))+logdet_C+logdet_info)
print('n, p, n-p:',len(y),x.shape[1],df)
print('q/(n-p):',reml_variance)
print('log determinant C:',logdet_C)
print('log determinant fixed information:',logdet_info)
print('Restricted log-likelihood:',reml_ll)
assert np.isclose(reml_ll,reference['log_likelihood'],rtol=0,atol=1e-8)

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Fixed-effect uncertainty
At the fitted variance components, the plug-in covariance is
\[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=\hat\sigma^2(X^\top C^{-1}X)^{-1}.\]
The fixed triangular QR block supplies this through triangular solves. Standard errors are square roots of its diagonal. Our mixed-model z tests and 95% intervals are normal Wald approximations; this does not supply finite-group Student t degrees of freedom or variance-component confidence intervals.

R_inv=solve_triangular(qr_fixed,np.eye(x.shape[1]))
cov_beta=reml_variance*R_inv@R_inv.T
matrix_tex(cov_beta,r'\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)')
print('Standard errors:',np.sqrt(cov_beta.diagonal()))
assert np.allclose(cov_beta,reference['covariance'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)

\(\displaystyle \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=\begin{bmatrix}46.575 & -1.4511 \\ -1.4511 & 2.3895\end{bmatrix}\)


Standard errors: [6.82455592 1.54578888]


The implementation is crates/stats-core/src/lmm.rs. Owned Vec inputs become nalgebra matrices; term/result structs preserve the array shapes and term order. Result propagates invalid designs, failed controls and nonconvergence to the PHP binding as exceptions. The binding validates and filters all aligned inputs, then returns plain arrays.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: Four grouping levels: which observations share variation?
text:
Four grouping levels: which observations share variation?
The same construction handles multiple nested terms. For repeated assessments within students, classes, schools and districts,
\[
y_i=x_i^\top\beta+d_{D(i)}+s_{S(i)}+c_{C(i)}+t_{T(i)}+\epsilon_i.
\]
Each term has its own Gaussian variance and is independent of the other terms. Conditional on the fixed design, two different observations share covariance only through common groups:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j\mid X)
=\tau_D^2\mathbf{1}_{D(i)=D(j)}
+\tau_S^2\mathbf{1}_{S(i)=S(j)}
+\tau_C^2\mathbf{1}_{C(i)=C(j)}
+\tau_T^2\mathbf{1}_{T(i)=T(j)},\quad i\ne j.
\]
On the diagonal, add the observation variance sigma² (or sigma²/w_i with weights). The grouping IDs must be globally unique within each term: a local school number needs its district in the key, and a local student number needs all its parents. Three grouping terms plus observations are often called a four-level model; here we name the number of grouping terms explicitly.

# Demonstrate the covariance implied by the fitted four-grouping-level model.
# This small matrix is for teaching; the native engine never constructs full V.
report=json.loads((ROOT/'docs/verifications/r-compatibility-results.json').read_text())
case=next(r for r in report['mixed'] if r['name']=='nested_4_grouping_levels_reml')
fit=case['PHP']['bobyqa']
input_case=next(r for r in fixtures['cases'] if r['name']==case['name'])
variances=np.array([t['covariance'][0][0] for t in fit['random']])
# First pair: same student; then different student, class, school and district.
selected=[0,1,4,8,16,32]
V=np.eye(len(selected))*fit['residual_variance']
for term,var in zip(input_case['terms'],variances):
    ids=np.array(term['groups'])[selected]
    V+=var*(ids[:,None]==ids[None,:])
display(pd.DataFrame(dict(grouping=['district','school','class','student'],
                          groups=[len(t['group_labels']) for t in fit['random']],
                          variance=variances)))
matrix_tex(V,r'V_{\mathrm{six\ observations}}')
print('Same student:',V[0,1])
print('Same class, different students:',V[0,2])
print('Same school, different classes:',V[0,3])
print('Same district, different schools:',V[0,4])
print('Different districts:',V[0,5])
assert np.isclose(V[0,1],variances.sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,2],variances[:3].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,3],variances[:2].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,4],variances[0])
assert V[0,5]==0

text: fit_ols() fits a linear model by least squares. fit_generalized_linear() fits a generalized linear model by maximum likelihood. Both take an R formula and named columns, as described in Model formulas.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Linear models

fit_ols() assumes independent errors with constant variance.
With weights, it fits weighted least squares, as lm(weights = ) does: each squared residual is multiplied by its row’s weight.
Intervals and tests use Student’s t with df_residual degrees of freedom.
The result adds t_statistics, rss, residual_variance, sigma, r_squared, and adj_r_squared to the shared keys.
fit_generalized_linear(family: 'gaussian') returns the same fit plus deviance, null_deviance, and aic, as R’s glm() reports them.

A first model shows a complete fit and its output.

Linear and generalized linear models
Linear and generalized linear models

Result keys

Key
Contents

Wald inference, in columns order

Each family’s matrix function in Matrix model functions defines these quantities exactly, including the null-deviance baseline and the convergence rule.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Weights and offsets

weights is an array aligned with the original rows, or the name of a numeric column.
Weights must be positive. A missing weight drops its row.
For fit_ols() and the Poisson family they are precision (prior) weights. For the binomial family they are integer trial counts, with the response given as proportions.
Offsets are written in the formula with offset(expr). Several offsets are added together.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Differences from R

A rank-deficient design throws code 1004. R reports aliased coefficients as NA.
Zero weights are rejected. R gives such rows zero weight.
Binomial and Poisson covariances are the inverse information at the final coefficients. R’s vcov() uses the IRLS weights of the iteration before the final one, so standard errors differ by about the size of R’s last step, up to about 1e-4 relative near separation. See GLM covariance.
Gaussian fit_generalized_linear() intervals use t, as fit_ols() does. R’s confint.default() uses z and confint() profiles the likelihood.

Model formulas lists the remaining differences in formula handling.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text: phit fits each model to complete rows. A row with a missing value in any variable the model uses is left out, the fit warns once, and the result records which input rows it used.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Behavior

missing: 'drop', the default, removes incomplete rows. missing: 'raise' throws instead, without fitting.
Only PHP null and NAN are missing. Infinities are errors, and strings such as '' or 'NA' are not treated as missing.
Formula fits check only the columns the formula uses, including weights, offsets, and grouping factors.
fitted and residuals hold one value per retained row, in retained_rows order. They are not padded with null.
Row positions count inputs in iteration order, from zero. They are not PHP array keys.
Every statistic, including df_residual, uses the retained rows.
phit does not impute values.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Interpreting a complete-case fit
Dropping incomplete rows changes the sample the model describes. Estimates can be biased when missingness is related to the outcome or the predictors. Report how many rows were dropped and why values are missing. phit offers no imputation or missing-data model.
R’s explicit na.action = na.omit and statsmodels’ explicit missing='drop' fit the same complete-case sample. They do not all warn by default. The warning and the row accounting are phit’s own contract. The three-implementation verification checks that phit, R, and statsmodels retain the same rows and give the same results.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Warning and accounting
A successful fit that drops rows emits one E_WARNING with the number dropped and the original sample size. In the polyfill it is an E_USER_WARNING. Complete data emits no warning. A failed fit throws and returns no accounting. The warning text is descriptive and is not a stable machine-readable interface.
Every successful result includes:







Key
Meaning




n_input
int: original observations


n_observations
int: retained observations used in estimation


n_dropped
int: omitted observations


retained_rows
list: original zero-based positions retained, ascending


dropped_rows
list: original zero-based positions omitted, ascending



To place residuals back at their original positions:
foreach ($result['retained_rows'] as $out => $in) {
    $residualAt[$in] = $result['residuals'][$out];
}
Log or display the warning with your normal warning handling, and use the counts for reporting. PHP settings can hide warnings, so applications should also check n_dropped. An error handler that turns warnings into exceptions aborts the call. Use missing: 'raise' to prohibit omission explicitly. Do not suppress the warning without recording the deletion.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Model-specific rules
Logistic. fit_logistic_matrix() follows the same deletion, warning, and row-accounting policy as fit_ols_matrix(). With default unit trial weights, numeric outcomes must be exactly 0 or 1, including rows with missing predictors. After deletion both classes must remain and n must exceed p. Residuals are response residuals, y minus the probability. Residuals and fitted probabilities follow retained_rows order.
Probit and Poisson. Probit follows the binary rules above. Poisson validates nonnegative integer counts before deletion, and at least one positive count must remain after it. Zero counts are observed values, not missing ones. Every estimator warns once on a successful fit that dropped rows, exposes original row positions, and supports missing: 'raise'.
Mixed-model group IDs. fit_mixed_gaussian_intercept_matrix() drops a row if x, y, or the group ID is missing. A missing group ID is null. NAN and float group IDs are invalid labels and are rejected. Group labels and sizes describe the retained sample, and a group removed entirely is absent from the results. If deletion leaves one group, only singleton groups, or too few observations for the fixed design, fitting fails. Use retained_rows to align conditional and population fitted values and both residual definitions with the original data.
Weights, offsets, and random terms. Optional weights and offsets, and every random term’s z and groups, share one listwise deletion mask. Their original lengths, types, and values are validated before deletion. Grouped-binomial proportions with positive integer trial weights are allowed. Invalid success or trial counts are errors, even in rows that would otherwise be dropped. General mixed fits warn once and return original row positions like the other functions. tests/r-compatibility.php and tests/lmm-expanded.php cover these cases.
Mixed logistic. fit_mixed_logistic_matrix() applies the same policy across x, proportions, groups, trial counts, and offsets. Trial counts above 1,000,000 are rejected before rows are dropped. Near-integer success encodings within tolerance are canonicalized only after validation and deletion. A sample with no successes or no failures then fails, since an unpenalized fit would not be finite.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Implementation
The PHP binding applies the omission policy before calling the Rust core. The Rust fit_ols() contract requires complete, finite numeric vectors.
Code that drops rows before calling phit must report that deletion itself, because phit can account only for the rows it receives.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Read a delimited text file into typed columns with read_csv(), or a chunk of rows at a time with CsvReader. The parsing rules follow readr 2 (readr::read_delim()) as phibble’s PHP reader implements them. These are the native readers behind phibble’s DataFrame::fromCsv(), csvChunks(), and fromCsvChunked().
The CSV readers need the extension. The polyfill does not provide them.
read_csv() is narrower than DataFrame::fromCsv(), which adds these in PHP around the native call:

Options
Phit\read_csv(string $path, array $options = []): array;
Every option is optional, and the defaults are readr’s.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Types



Code
Type
Stored as




?
Guess



l
bool
PHP bool


i
int
PHP int


d
double
PHP float


c
string
PHP string


D
date
int: days since 1970-01-01


T
datetime
int: microseconds since the epoch, UTC


_
Skip
The column is null




Guessing
Values are trimmed and mapped to missing first. The guess uses every row when there are at most guess_max. Otherwise it uses guess_max - 1 evenly spaced rows (step = intdiv(rows, guess_max): rows 0, step, 2·step, and so on) plus the last row, as vroom does. The first rule that fits every sampled value wins.

bool: T F TRUE FALSE True False true false t f.
int: an optional sign, then digits with optional grouping marks between them, that fits in 64 bits. An unsigned leading zero (007) stays text, while 0 and -07 are ints.
double: [+-]inf or [+-]nan in any case, or a decimal number with an optional decimal mark, exponent, and grouping marks. 1. and 1, qualify. The leading-zero rule applies, so 0e5 and 00.5 stay text.
date: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY/MM/DD. The two separators may differ.
datetime: YYYY-MM-DD[(T| )HH[:MM[:SS[.fraction]]]][Z|±HH[[:]MM]].
Otherwise string.


A column that is entirely missing, with at least one data row, is bool.
Whole numbers guess as int, where readr guesses double.
The date and datetime rules check only the shape. A column of date-shaped values guesses date even if one is not a calendar date, and that value then fails to parse.



Parsing
The column’s type applies to every row. A guessed numeric column allows the grouping mark. An explicitly typed one does not, as in phibble.







Type
Accepts




bool
The guessing values, plus 1 and 0


int
Leading zeros and a + sign


double
PHP numeric strings (when the decimal mark is .), inf, nan, and the guessing grammar


date
A valid calendar date in years 0001 to 9999


datetime
A valid date, hours up to 23, minutes and seconds up to 59



For datetimes:

Fractions are truncated to microseconds.
An offset converts to UTC, and no offset means UTC. Offsets up to ±24:59 are accepted, as PHP’s DateTimeImmutable accepts them.
A date alone is midnight UTC.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Missing values

A value that matches an na string after trimming is missing and becomes null. A quoted "NA" is also missing.
A value that does not parse as its column’s type also becomes null, and it is counted in the column’s failed.
Short rows are padded with missing values.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Result
[
    'names' => list<string>,
    'columns' => list<null|array{
        type: 'bool'|'int'|'float'|'string'|'date'|'datetime',
        values: list<bool|int|float|string|null>,
        failed: int,
    }>,
    'problems' => list<string>,
]

Values use phibble’s storage forms, listed under Types. A skipped column is null.
failed counts values that did not parse under the column’s type. phibble turns nonzero counts into column 'x': n values could not be parsed as type problems.
problems holds one entry per ragged row, such as row 7: expected 5 columns, got 4. A file that ends inside a quoted field adds row N: unterminated quoted field at end of file.
A problem’s row number is the record’s position in the file, counting skipped lines and the header. A multi-line quoted field counts as one record.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Records

Long rows put the extra fields, joined by the delimiter, into the last column.
A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the file is removed before tokenizing when skip is 0, so a quoted first header loses its quotes. A mark at the start of the first record after skipped lines is also removed.
LF and CRLF line endings are accepted. CR is the line ending when the first line break falls in a 4 MiB stretch of the file (counted from the first byte after skipped lines) that holds no LF. Otherwise a lone CR is data. phibble decides from its first 4 MiB block with a line break, so the two readers agree.
Quoted fields can hold delimiters and line breaks, which are kept as written.
An unterminated quote at the end of the file closes the field there.
Bytes pass through unchanged. There is no encoding validation.

A line is blank when its raw text holds only spaces, tabs, and carriage returns.

The test uses the raw line, not the parsed fields. A quoted empty string is data, and the result does not depend on trim_ws or the delimiter: a line of spaces is blank even when the delimiter is a space.
With skip_empty_rows, a blank line is dropped. Otherwise it is tokenized like any other line, so an empty line is one empty field, and in a wider file the record is reported as one column short.
An unterminated last line is never dropped, so a\n is two rows and a\n \n is one.

An empty file, or one with only empty lines, returns no names and no columns. When the header is read but no data rows are, the names come back with empty columns typed string, as readr reads a header-only file as text. That happens with n_max: 0, a header-only file, a skip that leaves no row after the header, and every row blank under skip_empty_rows. An explicit code in types still applies.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Reading in chunks
Phit\CsvReader reads a file a chunk of rows at a time, as readr’s read_delim_chunked() does. Its memory follows the chunk size, not the file size.
$reader = new Phit\CsvReader(string $path, array $options = []);
$reader->names(): array;           // list<string>
$reader->next(int $rows): ?array;  // the next chunk, or null

The options are read_csv()’s.
The constructor reads the header, so names() works before the first chunk. It returns the header’s names, X1..Xn when col_names is false, or [] for an empty file.
next() returns at most $rows rows in read_csv()’s result shape, plus position (the 1-based index of the chunk’s first row) and rows (the chunk’s row count). It returns null once no rows remain.
Types not given in types are guessed from the first chunk, from guess_max of its rows sampled as above. Later chunks use those types, and a value that does not fit counts in that chunk’s failed. phibble sets guess_max to the chunk size by default, as readr does.
Problem rows are numbered from the start of the file, and each chunk carries the problems of its own rows.
The unterminated-quote problem goes with the last chunk. After each chunk, the reader looks past blank lines to see whether records remain.
n_max caps the rows across all chunks.
A file with no data rows gives no chunks. The exception is an unterminated quote in the header: next() then returns a chunk with no rows that carries the problem.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Errors
A missing or unreadable file, or an invalid option, throws \ValueError, not the statistical exception. Invalid options include:

an unknown key or a wrong value type
a multi-byte delimiter, quote, decimal mark, or grouping mark
an unknown type code
a negative skip or n_max
decimal and grouping marks that are equal, or that are a digit, sign, e, E, or newline

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Differences from readr
These follow phibble’s reader:

Whole numbers guess as int.
With a comment prefix, a value followed by a comment is trimmed, so 2 # x reads as 2.
Date and datetime guessing checks the shape only.
In a file whose only line ending is CR, readr skips a blank line only before the first record and keeps interior and trailing ones. Both phit and phibble read CR as the line ending and apply the blank-line rule throughout.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Implementation notes

Tokenizers
phibble tokenizes with vroom’s (readr 2’s) quote rules. It uses a fast reader when it can (no comment, "" escapes, no backslash escapes, and a quote character) and its own character-level reader otherwise. The native reader reproduces both, including their differences:

In the fast reader, a field is quoted when its first byte is the quote. Inside it, every lone quote toggles quoting and is dropped, and a doubled quote is a literal quote, so "x "y" z" reads as x y z. Quotes in an unquoted field are literal.
The character-level reader folds CRLF to LF everywhere, including inside quotes. A quote opens a quoted section only when the field so far is whitespace. Text after the comment prefix ends the record, so a line holding only spaces and a comment is a one-field record holding those spaces. Before the first record, a comment prefix with only whitespace before it drops the line, as in readr.



Memory and passes

read_csv() reads 65,536 rows at a time and converts each block to PHP values before reading the next, so it holds one block of the file’s text at a time.
When any column’s type is guessed, it first reads the file twice more: once to count the rows, and once to collect the rows it guesses from, which are spread across the whole file. Giving every column’s type in types skips those two passes.
A string repeated in a column is stored as one shared PHP string.
CsvReader holds the text of one chunk and one read block.



Timing
phibble’s 1,000,000-row benchmark file (46 MB: an int ID, an int key, a string label, a float with about 2% NA, and a datetime) was read with guessed types, each reader in its own process. The machine was a 2-core AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX virtual machine with Ubuntu 24.04 and PHP 8.5.12. Times are the median of five reads after one warm-up, and memory is the peak RSS of the whole process. The raw record keeps every timing.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Verification







Suite
Checks




tests/csv.php
Quoting, escapes, missing values, trimming, every option and type code, guessing, datetimes, ragged rows, chunks, and errors


tests/csv-conformance.php
read_csv() and CsvReader against phibble’s reader on a fixed corpus, without a phibble checkout


tests/csv-phibble.php
Both readers through phibble on the corpus and on random files; runs when PHIBBLE_AUTOLOAD is set



Conformance corpus. phibble generates tests/fixtures/csv-conformance.json from its PHP reader with bin/generate-csv-conformance, and this repository commits a byte-identical copy.

The 108 cases cover every option at its default and one other value, all eight type codes, ragged rows, a byte order mark, CRLF and CR endings, an unterminated quote, comments, an empty file, invalid UTF-8, the four ways to read no data rows, and eighteen shapes of the blank-line rule.
Each case records the input, options, names, types, values, failure counts, and problems. read_csv() must reproduce all of it, so a change in either reader fails in its own repository.
Every case is read again at block sizes of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 64 bytes, and through CsvReader in one chunk and in chunks of 1, 2, and 3 rows. One chunk must equal the whole read. Small chunks must give the same problems in order and, read as text, the same values.
phibble does not report an unterminated quoted field, and read_csv() does. Each case lists the extra problems read_csv() may add, and the suite compares against that union, so any other problem fails.
tests/fixtures/PHIBBLE_REFERENCE pins the phibble commit. bin/fetch-csv-fixtures copies the file from that commit, using a local checkout given as its first argument or in PHIBBLE_REPO, or a clone of the pinned repository. To refresh, regenerate the corpus in phibble, move the pin, and run the script.

phibble tier. tests/csv-phibble.php compares both readers through DataFrame::fromCsv() on the corpus and on random files and options. CSV_FUZZ_CASES and CSV_FUZZ_SEED set the count and seed. Names, types, values, and warnings must be identical. With a phibble that has DataFrame::csvChunks(), it also compares CsvReader with phibble’s chunked reader over random files, chunk sizes, and block sizes (CSV_CHUNK_CASES of them). Chunks, positions, types, values, and per-chunk warnings must match in order.

title: phit
text:
Fit statistical models, compute probability distributions, and summarize data in PHP. Model functions accept formulas or explicit designs and return PHP arrays.
Formulas follow R: rent ~ area + district models rent from floor area and district. phit builds the numeric design from named columns, including factors, interactions, and transformations such as log(area).
A first model runs this example with its data.

title: phit
text:
Capabilities



Area
Functions
Guide




Linear and generalized linear models
fit_ols(), fit_generalized_linear(): linear, logistic, probit, and Poisson regression with weights and offsets
Models

Mixed models

Reading CSV files



Each model also has a matrix function, such as fit_ols_matrix(), for code that builds its own design. See Matrix model functions.

title: phit
text:
Results

Coefficient names, treatment contrasts, term order, deviance, and AIC follow R’s lm() and glm(). Mixed models follow lme4.
Rows with missing values are dropped with a warning, and every result reports which rows it used.
Errors are PHP exceptions with stable numeric codes.
The verification pages compare each model with R, lme4, and statsmodels and record the tolerances.

title: phit
text:
Requirements
phit runs on non-thread-safe PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5 on Linux and macOS. It installs with PIE or from prebuilt Linux binaries (Installation). Where the extension cannot be installed, the plain-PHP polyfill provides every function except the CSV reader, and runs more slowly.

title: Model formulas
text:
The formula functions take an R model formula and a data set of named columns. They build R’s model matrix and fit it with the same estimators as the matrix functions. Each result has its matrix function’s complete contract plus coefficient names.
PHP reflection reports $data and $weights as mixed. The stubs in stubs/phit.php document the accepted types.

title: Model formulas
Model formulas
text:
Data
$data is an associative array of columns, name => list of values. An object is also accepted: phit calls its public toModelData() method, or toColumns() when that is absent, and uses the returned array. Exceptions from those methods propagate unchanged. phibble’s DataFrame::toModelData() returns this shape.
Each column is one of the following.

Numbers: integers and floats. null and NAN are missing. Infinity raises 1003.
Booleans: a logical column. R codes it as a two-level factor named {col}TRUE.
Strings: a character column. It becomes a factor whose levels are the distinct retained values in byte (C-locale) order, which is R’s order under LC_COLLATE=C. Other R locales can sort mixed-case or accented strings differently.
A factor descriptor: an array with exactly the keys levels (list of unique strings), codes (list of 0-based integers, null for missing), and ordered (bool). Levels keep the caller’s order and the first level is the reference.
Dates arrive as numbers, for example days or seconds since the epoch.
Every column must have the same length (code 1002).
Only the columns a formula uses are type-checked.
An unknown column, a malformed factor descriptor, a referenced list-column or mixed-type column, or a list of row arrays raises 1001.

title: Model formulas
text:
Formula syntax
The formula grammar and operator precedence follow R.







Syntax
Meaning




y ~ a + b
Main effects. ~ a + b (no response) is valid for model_matrix.


- 1, + 0, 0 +
Remove the intercept. + 1 restores it.


a:b
Interaction columns for every combination of the coded variables.


a * b
a + b + a:b.


(a + b + c)^2
All main effects and interactions up to order 2.


a / b
a + a:b (nesting). b %in% a is b:a.


- term
Remove a term, for example a * b - a:b.


.
Every data column that does not appear in the response.


offset(expr)
A fixed known offset. Several offsets are summed.


(x | g), (x || g)
Random-effect terms (see below).



Terms are ordered as R orders them: main effects first, then two-way interactions, and so on, with ties in formula order. Within an interaction, variables appear in order of first appearance in the formula, and the first variable varies fastest in the column order. y ~ b:a + a therefore gives bv:ap, bv:aq, and so on.

Inline transforms
The following functions can appear as variables or inside one another. Column names are R’s deparsed expressions, including R’s spacing and its 15-digit number formatting, for example I(x^2), I(area/beds), I(x * 1e+05), and log(x, base = 2).

log(x), log(x, base), log2, log10, log1p, exp, expm1, sqrt, abs, sin, cos, and tan.
I(expr) with + - * / ^, numbers, parentheses, unary minus, comparisons (< > <= >= == !=), &, |, and !. A comparison gives a logical column, such as I(x > 3)TRUE. Strings compare with character and factor columns: I(region == "north").
poly(x, degree) gives R’s orthogonal polynomials and poly(x, degree, raw = TRUE) gives raw powers. Columns are named poly(x, 2)1, poly(x, 2)2, and so on. Orthogonal polynomials are computed over all input rows before deletion, as in R, and reject missing values. Raw polynomials allow them.
factor(x), as.factor(x), and ordered(x) convert a column. Numeric levels are sorted numerically and labelled with R’s number formatting. Levels come from all input rows, as in R’s model frame.
as.numeric(f) gives 1-based factor codes.
cbind(successes, failures) is a binomial response for fit_generalized_linear and fit_mixed_logistic.

Any other function raises 1007. A transform result of NaN, such as log(-1), is missing and is deleted like any other missing value (R also removes it, with a “NaNs produced” warning). An infinite result, such as log(0), raises 1003.


Contrasts
Unordered factors, strings, and logicals use treatment contrasts. The columns are named {variable}{level} for every level after the first. Ordered factors use contr.poly, with columns .L, .Q, .C, ^4, and so on. R’s coding rule decides whether a factor in a term receives contrasts or one indicator per level. A factor is coded by contrasts when the term without it appears earlier in the formula, or is empty. Without an intercept, the first factor in the first term that contains one receives full indicator coding. These rules give R’s columns for formulas such as y ~ 0 + f, y ~ x:f, y ~ f:g, and y ~ f * g - 1.

title: Model formulas
text:
Missing values and unused levels

Listwise deletion uses only the variables the formula references: the response, transforms, offsets, weights, grouping factors, and random-effect columns. Other columns may contain missing values.
missing: 'drop' removes incomplete rows with one E_WARNING. missing: 'raise' raises 1001. Missing values describes the warning and the row accounting.
model_matrix keeps unused factor levels, as R’s model.matrix() does. Their indicator columns are all zero.
The fitting functions drop levels that are absent after deletion, as lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() do through drop.unused.levels = TRUE.
Character levels always come from the retained rows.

title: Model formulas
text:
model_matrix
The result has these keys.







Key
Contents




y
Response values. A factor response gives 0-based codes plus response_levels. cbind(s, f) gives [s, f] rows. null without a response.


x
Design rows for retained observations, including (Intercept) when present.


columns, assign
R column names and R’s assign attribute (0 for the intercept).


terms, intercept
R term labels and whether the intercept is present.


formula, response
The deparsed formula and response expression.


offset
Summed offsets, or null.


random
One entry per random-effect term: label, group, columns, correlated, z, groups.


n_input, n_observations, n_dropped, retained_rows, dropped_rows
Deletion accounting.



x includes the intercept column, so pass it to a matrix function with intercept: false. Each random entry has the shape that fit_mixed_gaussian_matrix expects:
$mm = Phit\model_matrix('y ~ x + (1 + x | g)', $data);
$fit = Phit\fit_mixed_gaussian_matrix(
    x: $mm['x'],
    y: $mm['y'],
    random: $mm['random'],
    intercept: false,
);

title: Model formulas
text:
fit_ols and fit_generalized_linear
fit_ols returns the full fit_ols_matrix result. fit_generalized_linear supports four family and link combinations. An empty link selects the canonical link.








Family
Links
Core




gaussian
identity
fit_ols_matrix, plus deviance, null_deviance, and aic as R’s glm() reports them


binomial
logit, probit
fit_logistic_matrix, fit_probit_matrix


poisson
log
fit_poisson_matrix




Other families or links raise 1007.
A binomial response can be 0/1 numbers, booleans, a factor or character column (the first level is failure and every other level is success, as in R), proportions with integer trial weights, or cbind(successes, failures).
$weights is an array aligned with the original rows, or the name of a numeric column. Weights must be positive, and a missing weight deletes its row.
Random-effect terms raise 1007 and name fit_mixed_gaussian and fit_mixed_gaussian_matrix as the alternatives.

Every formula fit adds these keys to the matrix result:







Key
Contents




formula, response
The deparsed formula and response expression


columns
Coefficient names, aligned with coefficients


named
column => coefficient


terms, assign, intercept
R term labels, R’s assign attribute, and whether an intercept is present


predvars
State that prediction reuses: each factor’s levels after deletion and each orthogonal poly() basis (R’s xlevels and predvars)


family, link
fit_generalized_linear and fit_mixed_logistic only

title: Model formulas
text:
fit_mixed_gaussian and fit_mixed_logistic
fit_mixed_gaussian fits lme4-style bar terms with the fit_mixed_gaussian_matrix estimator. REML is the default, as in lme4::lmer().







Bar term
Meaning




(1 | g)
Random intercept


(x | g), (0 + x | g)
Correlated random intercept and slope; slope only


(x || g)
Uncorrelated intercept and slope (diagonal covariance)


(1 | g1) + (1 | g2)
Several independent terms


(1 | g1:g2)
Interaction groups


(1 | g1/g2)
Nesting: (1 | g1) + (1 | g2:g1), with lme4’s group name and g2level:g1level labels




The result is the fit_mixed_gaussian_matrix contract. Each random entry also has label, group, columns, and correlated.
effects_cond_var lists one k×k conditional covariance per group, in group_labels order. These are the blocks that ranef(fit, condVar = TRUE) attaches as postVar. For (x || g), lme4 reports only the diagonal of each block.

fit_mixed_logistic supports exactly one random intercept (1 | g) with the binomial family and logit link, using the fit_mixed_logistic_matrix estimator.

quadraturePoints is lme4’s nAGQ.
Responses follow fit_generalized_linear.
random_effects_cond_var is the conditional variance of each group’s mode, as lme4’s postVar.

title: Model formulas
text:
Prediction: predict
predict($fit, $newdata) predicts from any formula fit, as R’s predict() does for lm, glm and merMod objects. It rebuilds the fit’s formula over $newdata, which needs the predictor columns but not the response.
$fit = Phit\fit_generalized_linear(
    'am ~ wt + poly(hp, 2)',
    $cars,
    family: 'binomial',
);
$p = Phit\predict(
    $fit,
    ['wt' => [2.2, 3.4], 'hp' => [95, 180]],
    type: 'response',
    seFit: true,
);
// $p['fit']: probabilities. $p['se_fit']: delta-method SEs.

Factors are coded with the levels the fit saw. A level the fit never saw raises 1001 with R’s message (factor g has new level z). Logical and character columns work the same way.
poly(x, k) evaluates the fitted orthogonal basis at the new values, as R’s predict.poly() does. It is not refitted to the new data.
offset() terms are evaluated over $newdata and added.
A row with a missing predictor predicts null and is listed in missing_rows. Every list has one entry per $newdata row.
type: 'link' (the default) returns the linear predictor. type: 'response' applies the inverse link, and seFit then uses the delta method, as R does.
interval: 'confidence' or 'prediction' adds lower and upper for fit_ols fits, using t with df_residual at level. A prediction interval adds the residual variance; as in R, it assumes constant variance for a weighted fit.
For fit_mixed_gaussian and fit_mixed_logistic fits, predictions add each known group’s random effects (lme4’s default re.form = NULL). random: false gives population predictions (re.form = NA), and the grouping columns can then be absent. An unseen group raises 1001 unless allowNewLevels: true, which predicts it at the population level. Mixed predictions have no standard errors, as in lme4.

GLM standard errors use the covariance at the final coefficients. R’s predict.glm() uses vcov(), which reuses the weights of the iteration before the final one, so the two differ by about the size of R’s last IRLS step. See GLM covariance.

title: Model formulas
text:
Differences from R

Character levels use byte order. R’s default locale collation can order mixed-case or non-ASCII strings differently.
Rank-deficient designs raise 1004. R reports NA (aliased) coefficients instead.
Weights must be positive. R accepts zero weights. cbind() rows with zero trials are rejected; R gives them zero weight.
A response that also appears on the right-hand side raises 1001. R drops the term with a warning.
Only the functions listed above can be evaluated. factor() takes one argument, and poly() takes one variable.
x %in% a is labelled x:a. R labels the term x %in% a; the columns are identical.
model_matrix returns factor responses as 0-based codes with response_levels.
fit_generalized_linear(family: 'gaussian') uses t-based intervals, as fit_ols_matrix does. R’s confint.default() is z-based and confint() profiles the likelihood.
fit_mixed_gaussian orders groups and effects by first appearance after deletion and keeps random terms in formula order. lme4 sorts levels and orders terms by their number of levels. Estimates are invariant to these orderings.
Duplicate column names collapse in the named map; columns keeps every name.

title: Model formulas
text:
Verification








Generator
References
Test and tolerance




tests/generate-formula-fixtures.R
62 under LC_COLLATE=C: 33 model.frame()/model.matrix() designs, 14 lm() fits, 15 glm() fits
tests/formula.php: columns, terms, and rows exact; design values within 1e-12 relative; fits within 1e-9 + 1e-7*abs(reference)


tests/generate-formula-lme4-fixtures.R
10 lme4 fits (7 lmer(), 3 glmer()), including ranef(condVar = TRUE)
tests/formula-mixed.php: the lme4 suites’ tolerances


tests/generate-predict-fixtures.R
25 predict() cases for lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer()
tests/predict.php: GLM standard errors tight against R’s final-coefficient value, 1e-3 relative against R’s se.fit




The formula data are the repository’s housing, schools, learning, clinic, and cbpp data, plus a seeded synthetic set with factors, unused and reordered levels, ordered factors, logicals, character columns, missing values, weights, offsets, transforms, and no-intercept models.
glm() references are restarted from R’s own solution until the coefficients stop changing, because R’s default deviance criterion fixes coefficients only to about the square root of its tolerance.
The prediction data include values outside the fitted range, missing rows, an unseen group, and a factor whose level set differs from the fit. tests/predict.php also checks that predicting the training data reproduces the fitted values.

All fixtures are indexed in the reference manifest.

title: Densities, quantiles, and random draws
text:
Notes

_pdf, _cdf, _quantile, and _sf correspond to R’s dnorm(), pnorm(), qnorm(), and pnorm(lower.tail = FALSE).
_sf keeps precision far into the upper tail, where 1 - cdf loses it.
Student’s t has heavier tails than the normal. Its values approach the normal’s as the degrees of freedom grow.
Each dist_normal_rng($n, $seed, $mean, $sd) call starts its own stream from the seed, so the same seed and parameters give the same draws.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text: Edit the Quarto .qmd sources in docs/, render them, and commit the rendered HTML with its sources. The statistical engine does not depend on Quarto, and the root README.md stays a short repository entry point.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Render and preview
Install the Quarto CLI (on macOS, brew install --cask quarto). The site is currently rendered with Quarto 1.10.18.
quarto preview docs
./scripts/render-docs
./scripts/render-docs runs quarto render docs and copies the result from docs/_site/ into docs/. quarto render docs alone writes only docs/_site/.

A full render reuses the saved results in docs/_freeze/, so it needs no Python, R, or built extension.
A render that reuses saved results checks presentation only. It is not a new numerical verification, and the walkthroughs show the versions from their last execution.
Rendering a single page executes its code, even when a full render would reuse the saved results. Quarto’s freeze documentation explains why. Any edit to a computational walkthrough, including a prose edit, needs a single-page render to update its frozen content.
A single-page render can remove docs/site_libs/ files that other pages still use. Finish with ./scripts/render-docs, or restore docs/site_libs/ from git.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Recompute the walkthroughs
Follow the development setup to select a matching PHP, and install R with Rscript on the PATH. The mixed-model references need R’s lme4, and the published-data comparison also needs nlme. These are development dependencies only.
Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("lme4", "nlme"),
  repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")'

python3 -m venv .context/notebooks-venv
.context/notebooks-venv/bin/pip install -r docs/notebooks/requirements.txt
export QUARTO_PYTHON="$PWD/.context/notebooks-venv/bin/python"
# macOS; on Linux use libphit.so and the matching PHP paths.
export PHP=/opt/homebrew/bin/php
export PHP_CONFIG=/opt/homebrew/bin/php-config
cargo build -p phit --locked
export STATS_EXTENSION="$PWD/target/debug/libphit.dylib"
Then run each model’s comparison script before rendering its notebooks:
PY=.context/notebooks-venv/bin/python
$PY docs/verifications/compare_ols.py
quarto render docs/notebooks/ols-math.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/ols-verification.qmd
$PY docs/verifications/compare_logistic.py
quarto render docs/notebooks/logistic-math.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/logistic-verification.qmd
$PY docs/verifications/compare_probit.py
$PY docs/verifications/compare_poisson.py
quarto render docs/notebooks/probit-math.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/probit-verification.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/poisson-math.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/poisson-verification.qmd
$PY docs/verifications/compare_lmm.py
quarto render docs/notebooks/lmm-math.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/lmm-verification.qmd
quarto render docs/notebooks/lmm-public-verification.qmd
quarto render docs/data/lmm/index.qmd
quarto render docs/benchmarks/lmm.qmd
./scripts/render-docs

Single-page renders execute every chunk in order and update _freeze/. The final step assembles the site.
RSCRIPT selects a non-default Rscript. QUARTO_PYTHON selects the virtual environment without putting machine-specific paths in the project configuration.
A change to input data or an estimator requires re-execution even if the prose is unchanged.
Review the .qmd, _freeze/, and comparison-report diffs together. The outputs record evidence from the environment used, not a guarantee for every platform.
The comparison scripts capture PHP warnings to keep their JSON valid, then show and check those warnings explicitly.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Writing a walkthrough
Each implemented estimator has a derivation walkthrough and an equivalent-model verification, following the notebook guide. Do not create placeholder notebooks for methods phit does not implement.

Use a small, reproducible simulated dataset with named variables, units, noise, and meaningful relationships. State its generating equation, seed, population parameters, and observed correlations. Save and share the observations, and label them synthetic. See the learning-data convention.
State the model’s assumptions and input ordering, derive the calculations before showing them, connect result fields to the production code, and explain edge cases.
Give equivalent R, statsmodels, and PHP calls where those references support the estimator. State differences in statistical conventions rather than silently adjusting one library’s results.
Keep assertions near the results and keep executed outputs. Share inputs with the reference tests where possible.


Authoring rules

Ordinary fenced blocks (python, r, php) are displayed only. {python} chunks execute in the Jupyter kernel; the comparison runners invoke R and PHP from Python.
Execution starts in docs/, and the code finds the repository root by locating Cargo.toml. A missing dependency or failed assertion must fail the render.
Use relative links to .qmd pages so Quarto rewrites them to HTML.
Keep local reference data and scripts next to the verification page.
Use a Quarto-aware editor. Generated .ipynb files are not maintained sources.

For a prose-only page, render the site and check navigation and local links. For a computational change, rerun the affected pages and comparison scripts, inspect the output, and run the Rust and PHP checks.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Example pages with charts
An example page with a chart includes _generated/{name}.md, which scripts/docs-examples.php writes from docs/examples/scripts/{name}.php.

The script runs in an empty directory beside this checkout’s vendor/, with the CSV files it names copied from docs/data.
The generated file holds the script without its opening tag and Composer bootstrap, its output, and its phiz chart. The downloadable script keeps the bootstrap.
phiz is a Composer dev dependency for this purpose only. The scripts also need the phit and phpolars extensions.

composer install
php -d extension=target/release/libphit.dylib \
    -d extension=/path/to/libphp_polars.dylib \
    scripts/docs-examples.php
Commit the generated files. Rendering the docs does not run the scripts.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Figures
Benchmark and notebook figures use the shared R and ggplot2 renderer described in Figure conventions. Python computes and verifies, and does not draw; Matplotlib is not a documentation dependency.
To refresh saved figures without estimating or timing anything:
Rscript docs/figures/render.R --all
./scripts/render-docs
The renderer reads saved reports and small point snapshots exported by the notebooks. Executing a single .qmd page calls the renderer when needed.

title: Building and maintaining the documentation
text:
Publishing
phpstats.org imports the rendered HTML committed under docs/, and GitHub Pages serves the same directory at https://phpstats.github.io/phit/. Neither runs Quarto.

Every page in the docs/_quarto.yml sidebar needs its rendered HTML committed.
After editing sources or refreshing frozen results, run ./scripts/render-docs and commit the HTML and assets with their sources.
docs/.nojekyll lets GitHub Pages serve directories whose names start with an underscore.

title: Development
text: Build phit from a checkout, run its tests, and change the implementation. To use phit in an application, see Installation. Run the commands from the repository root.

title: Development
text:
Environment
The setup follows the official ext-php-rs installation guide and Hello World build workflow:
# macOS: Xcode command-line tools, Rust, PHP (includes headers), libclang
xcode-select --install
brew install rust php llvm
export PHP="$(brew --prefix php)/bin/php"
export PHP_CONFIG="$(brew --prefix php)/bin/php-config"
export PATH="$(brew --prefix php)/bin:$PATH"
# If bindgen cannot find libclang:
export LIBCLANG_PATH="$(brew --prefix llvm)/lib"
Linux (Debian or Ubuntu with PHP 8.3, 8.4 or 8.5 in the configured repositories):
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential clang libclang-dev php-cli php-dev curl
# Install stable Rust using https://rustup.rs, then source ~/.cargo/env.
export PHP="$(command -v php)"
export PHP_CONFIG="$(command -v php-config)"

Check php -v, php-config --version, and rustc --version.
php and php-config must come from the same installation, with the same architecture, thread safety, and debug mode.
scripts/check and scripts/check-fpm take PHP from php-config --php-binary unless PHP is set, so another php earlier on PATH, such as Herd’s, does not affect them. Commands you run by hand still need the matching php.
On macOS, the linker configuration lets PHP resolve symbols when it loads the extension. Linux needs no extra linker flags.

With Homebrew LLVM’s libclang on macOS, also select the matching compiler and header directory. Xcode’s older arm_neon.h with a newer libclang fails to build:
export LIBCLANG_PATH="$(brew --prefix llvm)/lib"
export CC="$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin/clang"
export CXX="$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin/clang++"
export BINDGEN_EXTRA_CLANG_ARGS="-resource-dir=$($CC -print-resource-dir) -isysroot=$(xcrun --show-sdk-path)"

title: Development
text:
Build and run
cargo test --workspace --locked
cargo build -p phit --locked
# macOS; on Linux the file is libphit.so.
export STATS_EXTENSION="$PWD/target/debug/libphit.dylib"
php -n -d "extension=$STATS_EXTENSION" -r 'echo phpversion("phit"), PHP_EOL;'
php -n -d "extension=$STATS_EXTENSION" tests/ols.php
php -n -d "extension=$STATS_EXTENSION" examples/ols.php

Each suite in tests/ and each script in examples/ runs the same way. ./scripts/check runs all of them.
-n skips the ini files, so the tests run against this build only.
To load the build permanently, run cargo build -p phit --release --locked and add extension=/absolute/path/to/target/release/libphit.dylib (Linux: .so) to the php.ini that php --ini shows. The optional cargo-php workflow (cargo install cargo-php --locked, then cargo php install --release from crates/php-extension) edits php.ini for you, so back it up first.
Rebuild for each PHP version.

Installation covers PIE and the prebuilt binaries. Deploying to servers covers containers and PHP-FPM, and Releasing covers release artifacts.

title: Development
text:
Numerical dependency policy

Linear algebra uses nalgebra’s Rust-native SVD, QR, Cholesky, triangular solves, and pivoted LU. There is one numerical path, with no BLAS or LAPACK dependency and no backend selection.
The general mixed fitter uses the pinned Rust-native bobyqa and argmin (Nelder–Mead) crates, which add no C, Fortran, BLAS, or LAPACK requirement.
An external numerical backend needs a concrete requirement that justifies the extra build and deployment work.

title: Development
text:
Changing the implementation

Keep statistical calculations in crates/stats-core and PHP conversion in crates/php-extension.
Use established numerical crates, and check their APIs against the versions in Cargo.lock.
Explain important mathematical steps next to the code.
Update the contracts and reference tests when behavior changes.
Do not add abstractions for hypothetical models.

./scripts/check runs the offline checks: Rust tests and clippy, every PHP suite and example, the stub and signature checks, the reference manifest, and the site export. Run it before pushing. Verification lists the further checks for each kind of change, and R compatibility covers regenerating R references.
CI runs the checks on macOS and Ubuntu, with fail-fast disabled so one platform’s failure does not cancel the other’s. The packaging workflow tests Linux x86_64 and aarch64 at PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5.

title: Descriptive statistics
text: Summarize PHP numeric arrays: means, variances, covariance and correlation, quantiles, weighted moments, kernel density estimates, interpolation, and the empirical CDF. The functions are stateless and return floats or packed lists.

title: Descriptive statistics

    string $missing = 'raise'): float;

    string $missing = 'raise'): array;

    array $values,
    string $missing = 'raise',
): float;
Phit\stat_weighted_mean(array $values, array $weights,
    string $missing = 'raise'): float;
Phit\stat_weighted_var(array $values, array $weights,
    string $type = 'frequency', string $missing = 'raise'): float;








type
Divisor
Minimum retained values




sample (default)
n − 1
Two


population
n
One for variance and SD, which return 0; two for covariance




Correlation needs at least two retained pairs. If either input is constant, it returns NAN, which marks the statistic as undefined.
Other summaries need at least one retained value.


Quantiles
Quantiles use R’s default type 7. For sorted values x, let h = 1 + (n − 1)p and interpolate between the adjacent values using the fractional part of h.

p must be in [0, 1]. p = 0 and p = 1 give the minimum and maximum.
The median is the type-7 quantile at p = 0.5.
stat_quantile_array sorts once and returns the same values as scalar calls, in the order of the probability array. An empty probability array returns [] after the values are validated.

title: Descriptive statistics
text:
Weights
Let \(W=\sum_i w_i\), \(m=\sum_i w_i x_i/W\), and \(SS=\sum_i w_i(x_i-m)^2\). Weights must be finite and nonnegative, and the retained total must be positive.








stat_weighted_var type
Definition
Use




frequency (default)
\(SS/(W-1)\)
Counts or replication weights; needs W > 1


reliability
\(SS/(W-\sum_i w_i^2/W)\)
Precision weights; needs a positive denominator


population
\(SS/W\)
Weighted population second moment




Integer frequency weights give the sample variance of the expanded sample.
Reliability and population results do not change when all weights are multiplied by a positive constant.
Zero weights are allowed. With one effective value, the population variance is 0 and the reliability variance is undefined.
A negative weight is rejected even when its paired value is missing. Weights align to original positions before deletion.
The draw moments API always normalizes weights and calls reliability normalization 'unbiased'. It never treats weights as counts.

Sums use Neumaier compensation, and variances and covariances use corrected two-pass centered moments. This keeps accuracy with large common offsets. The calculations are binary64 and have no extended precision.

title: Descriptive statistics
section: Density estimation, interpolation, and the ECDF
text:
Density estimation, interpolation, and the ECDF
Five functions follow R’s density(), bw.nrd0(), bw.nrd(), approx(), and ecdf(), with R’s argument names.
$draws = Phit\dist_normal_rng(4000, 7, 0.3, 0.05);
$d = Phit\stat_density($draws);
$at = [0.25, 0.3, 0.35];
$heights = Phit\stat_approx($d['x'], $d['y'], $at);
$below = Phit\stat_ecdf($draws, [0.0]); // Share at or below 0.
Phit\stat_density(array $x, string|float $bw = 'nrd0',
    float $adjust = 1.0, string $kernel = 'gaussian',
    int $n = 512, ?float $from = null, ?float $to = null,
    float $cut = 3.0, ?array $weights = null,
    string $missing = 'raise'): array;
Phit\stat_bw_nrd0(array $x, string $missing = 'raise'): float;
Phit\stat_bw_nrd(array $x, string $missing = 'raise'): float;
Phit\stat_approx(array $x, array $y, array $xout,
    string $method = 'linear', int $rule = 1,
    string $ties = 'mean', float $f = 0.0,
    string $missing = 'raise'): array;
Phit\stat_ecdf(array $x, array $q,
    string $missing = 'raise'): array;
stat_density() returns ['x' => list, 'y' => list, 'bw' => float, 'n' => int]. It follows R’s algorithm: the data are binned linearly onto a grid of at least 512 points (the next power of two above n), convolved with the kernel by FFT, and interpolated onto n points from from to to.







Option
Values




bw
'nrd0' (Silverman’s rule, default), 'nrd' (Scott’s variation), or a positive number; multiplied by adjust


kernel
gaussian, epanechnikov, rectangular, triangular, biweight, cosine, optcosine


from, to
Default to the data range extended by cut bandwidths


weights
Used as given, as in R; weights that sum to one are renormalized after missing values are dropped




The automatic bandwidths ignore weights, as R’s do.
R’s ucv, bcv, and SJ bandwidths are not available.

stat_approx() sorts the points by x and collapses tied x values by ties ('mean', 'min', or 'max').

method: 'linear' interpolates linearly. method: 'constant' uses a step function in which f weights the right-hand value.
Outside the data range, rule: 1 returns NAN and rule: 2 returns the value at the nearer end.

stat_ecdf() returns the proportion of x at or below each q.

x, y, and weights follow the missing-value policy above, and pairs are dropped together.
Evaluation points (xout and q) may be infinite. A null or NAN evaluation point returns NAN, as R returns NA.

title: Published mixed-model verification data: provenance
text:
Sleep deprivation
sleepstudy.csv contains reaction times in milliseconds over ten days for eighteen subjects. All 180 rows are retained. Our verification model uses a fixed intercept, Days and a random intercept by Subject. The lme4 dataset documentation attributes the data to Belenky et al. (2003). Its example uses random slopes; our chosen random-intercept comparison is a different, deliberately simpler model.

title: Published mixed-model verification data: provenance
text:
Orthodontic growth
Orthodont.csv contains 108 measurements from 27 children. We use age, an explicitly constructed female indicator and age × female, with a random intercept by Subject. All observations and original columns are retained. Female=1 for Sex equal to ‘Female’; Male is the reference category. The nlme dataset documentation describes the measurements and cites Potthoff and Roy (1964), and Pinheiro and Bates (2000), Appendix A.17.

title: Published mixed-model verification data: provenance
text:
Worker and machine productivity
Machines.csv contains 54 observations: six workers each operated three machine brands three times. We construct separate B and C indicators, with A as the reference brand, and a random intercept by Worker. All rows and original columns are retained. This comparison has no worker-by-machine random interaction. The nlme documentation cites Milliken and Johnson (1992), and Pinheiro and Bates (2000), Appendix A.14.

title: Published mixed-model verification data: provenance
text:
High School and Beyond
Hsb82.csv contains all 7,185 observations in the package’s 1982 High School and Beyond sample. We retain the five columns used by the model: school, individual SES, school mean SES, school sector and mathematics achievement. The fixed columns are intercept, SES, mean SES and Catholic=1 for sector equal to ‘Catholic’; Public is the reference. School is the grouping variable, with 160 schools and 14–67 students per school. The mlmRev reference manual describes the data and cites Raudenbush and Bryk (2002), chapter 4.

title: Published mixed-model verification data: provenance
text:
Snapshot and model construction
The exporter tests/export-lmm-public-data.R reads installed package data and writes UTF-8 CSVs with original row order and no row-name column. The fixture generator tests/generate-lmm-public-fixtures.py constructs the numeric designs listed above, maps first-appearance group labels to integer core IDs, and saves lme4 and nlme ML reference outputs. The PHP verification also exercises original string labels. No rows are sampled or silently removed. The fixtures use explicit numeric designs so every implementation receives identical columns. Applications can pass the same data to fit_mixed_gaussian() with a formula instead.
The snapshots are distributed from packages declaring GPL (>= 2); package source links and study citations are in sources.json, and COPYING contains GPL version 2. These package distribution notices do not claim new ownership of the original studies. R and these data packages are development dependencies.
To intentionally refresh snapshots and expectations:
Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("lme4", "nlme", "mlmRev"), repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")'
.context/notebooks-venv/bin/python tests/generate-lmm-public-fixtures.py --export
To regenerate expectations from the existing, checksum-verified snapshots, omit --export; only lme4 and nlme are needed in R. Review CSVs, sources.json, tests/fixtures/lmm-public-r.json and the executed comparison together. A changed source snapshot must never be accepted solely by changing its hash.

title: Seeded sampling verification and performance
text:
Independent verification first
Before any timing phase, Python independently computes the ChaCha blocks at 17 evenly spaced indices, with the pinned PCG seed expansion/Open01 mapping. Base-R quantiles transform those exact probabilities. PHP’s sampled points must match at 1e-15 + 1e-12*abs(reference); discrete values match the integer quantiles. The full output is consumed by mean/variance calculations and checked against theoretical moments within eight standard errors (using the distribution’s fourth central moment for variance). Fixed seeds make these checks deterministic.
This complements the ordinary 25-case independent stream/quantile fixture suite. It does not compare every element to R and does not claim that R’s own RNG shares the ChaCha sequence. Each timed result undergoes the same numerical checks again.

Simulation and agreement
After the common benchmark setup, visitor counts are integers uniform from 80 to 300, and staffing is visitors/50 plus normal noise with standard deviation 0.8, clipped. The wider case adds independent standard-normal scores. Outcomes are draws from
\[\mu_i=\exp(0.1+0.005\,\mathrm{visitors}_i-0.12\,\mathrm{staff}_i
+0.1\sum_j\mathrm{extra}_{ij}),\qquad y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i).\]
This simulation is separate from the small teaching sample. Data hashes, generating coefficients, and sample correlations are recorded.
Coefficient-level quantities and scalar statistics are compared with R at 1e-9 + 1e-7 * abs(reference). Fitted values and residuals are computed in full and compared at ten evenly spaced rows; the small fixtures compare full vectors. phit must report convergence within 1 to 100 updates. Wald intervals follow R confint.default(), and the null baseline follows the documented intercept convention. Poisson deviance uses the saturated count likelihood, not −2 log-likelihood.

title: Random-intercept Gaussian ML scale validation and performance
text:
Algorithm
phit follows lme4’s penalized least-squares elimination. It separates within-group deviations from group means and caches an augmented QR square-root summary, so each trial variance ratio factors p + 1 + G rows rather than all n. Covariance is computed only for the selected solution. The walkthrough derives the reduction and checks its residual norms numerically.
phit uses nalgebra QR and SVD with no BLAS, LAPACK, or sparse backend. lme4 uses a general sparse Cholesky factorization; phit’s specialized reduction applies the same elimination and keeps SVD rank checks.

title: Random-intercept Gaussian ML scale validation and performance
text:
Timing boundaries and methods
Timed calls include estimation, fixed-effect covariance and normal Wald inference, variance components, ICC, likelihood/AIC, all population/conditional fits and both residual vectors, and all conditional group estimates. PHP also validates/copies inputs and converts all output arrays and group and sample metadata inside the timer.
R uses lmer REML=FALSE with bobyqa rhoend=1e-10. Python uses MixedLM ML BFGS with gtol=1e-10 and recalculates plug-in GLS covariance to align with the documented convention. Its own joint observed-Hessian covariance is a different convention and is not compared. Rust scans a log-ratio profile grid and refines analytic-score roots with compact weighted SVD GLS fits, after a one-time QR reduction. The algorithms and stopping rules differ, so this compares complete API calls, not one common solver.

title: Random-intercept Gaussian ML scale validation and performance
text:
Simulation and numerical checks
NumPy RNG seed 20261011 generates correlated study hours and prior scores, independent standard-normal extra predictors, and schools with roughly equal sizes. Outcomes follow
\[y_i=50+1.8\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.2\,\mathrm{prior}_i
+0.5\sum_j\mathrm{extra}_{ij}+b_{g(i)}+\epsilon_i,
\quad b_g\sim N(0,6^2),\quad\epsilon_i\sim N(0,5^2).\]
This sample is separate from the saved small teaching dataset. Identical 17-significant-digit CSVs are used by every worker. All coefficient-level fields, variance components, ICC, likelihood/AIC and all group effects are checked. Observation-length outputs are fully materialized, but cross-runtime checks sample ten evenly spaced rows; small fixtures check every row.
Benchmark absolute tolerance is 1e-7. Relative tolerance is 1e-6 for ordinary outputs, 1e-5 for covariance, SE, z-statistics, variance components, sigma, ICC, and random effects, and 1e-9 for likelihood/AIC. Small saved references use the tighter uniform 1e-7 + 1e-6 × abs(reference) policy. These tolerances apply to phit against R. statsmodels is checked against R as a peer, at 1e-6 + 1e-5 × abs(reference). At a million rows the profiled likelihood cannot separate variance ratios that differ by about 1e-6 relative: lme4’s deviance at R’s and at phit’s solutions differs by 7e-8 on 6.06 × 10^6. Independent optimizers stop at different points in that range, and the shrunken random effects move with the ratio, so they share the variance-sensitive tolerance.
At 100,000 rows, R’s between-group variance differed from the analytic-score solution by about 2.6e-6 relative while log-likelihood differed by only about 8e-10. The log-ratio profile score was approximately 2.55e-4 in R, -1.88e-6 in Python and 3.12e-11 in Rust. A flat likelihood and the floating-point resolution of the objective limit how closely independently optimized variance components agree, and the variance-sensitive tolerances above reflect that measurement. Likelihood agreement keeps its tight tolerance. The finite profile grid is not a proof of global optimality.
