title: Distribution performance
text:
Timing boundaries and interpretation
Distribution calls allocate and populate the complete output vector. The PHP scalar loop constructs a distribution and crosses the PHP/native boundary for each value; batch calls construct it once and stream values natively. The internal Rust loop uses the same validation and an allocated result vector. Descriptive mean/variance has one PHP native call; there is no invented scalar-loop equivalent for those operations.
JSON I/O, startup and output summaries are outside timed calls. PHP input/output conversion and native validation are included. R/SciPy start with native numeric vectors. Runtime reclamation/garbage collection of prior results contributes to the observed API cost. Peak RSS is the whole worker process, including imports, JSON parsing, inputs, outputs and summaries, not isolated kernel memory. Process elapsed time and input loading time are recorded separately.
R’s timer has millisecond resolution. Small distribution cases batch 100 calls; mean/variance batch enough calls to process at least ten million input values per measurement, with a minimum of ten calls. Per-call times divide by the batch count. All raw timings must be positive. The thread settings do not make different numerical implementations equivalent. PHP scalar and batch worker order alternates by case. Machine load, timer precision, and garbage collection affect the measurements, which describe these workloads only.

Reproduction and timing boundaries
Build using the matching PHP/header environment, then run:
cargo build -p phit --release --locked
# R and jsonlite are benchmark-only development dependencies.
PHP=/opt/homebrew/bin/php python3 tests/benchmarks/run-draws.py
# Optional overrides: RSCRIPT, STATS_EXTENSION; --repeats 5 --output /path/report.json
Python 3’s standard library generates inputs with random.Random(20261012). Draws have a shared Gaussian component, independent Gaussian noise and parameter means increasing by 0.1. Nonuniform weights have deterministic zeros every 11th row. Covariances are constructed from deterministic full-rank lower factors. The affine matrix includes off-diagonal mixing and a reflection, with a nonzero shift. Temporary JSON inputs are identical for PHP and R; their SHA-256 hashes are retained in the report. No intercept column is added.
Each worker loads JSON once. Startup, input generation, JSON parsing/serialization and reference comparison are outside timed calls. Input loading is recorded separately. Both APIs compute complete result arrays/matrices in each timed call; PHP includes native input conversion, validation and result allocation. Timings also include ordinary runtime reclamation of prior results.
R’s elapsed timer has millisecond resolution. Each map measurement batches 1,000 calls. Moments/affine batch 1,000 calls for the 1,000 × 4 case, 100 for 4,000 × 16, and 10 for both larger cases; the reported value divides by the batch count. This avoids zero small-call readings but still limits R timing precision. R’s garbage collection and machine load contribute variation; raw measurements are available for review. This run does not measure peak memory, Linux, PHP-FPM, Stan evaluation, PSIS or complete moment-matching iterations.

title: Binomial random-intercept scale checks and performance
text:
Timing boundaries and correctness
PHP times the complete native call, including conversion and all returned inference/observation arrays. R/Python materialize covariance, standard errors, conditional modes and full fixed/conditional fitted values and residuals. Process time includes startup, CSV load, warm-up and all timed fits.
A report is written only after coefficients, covariance/standard errors, group SD/modes, normalized likelihood and common observation samples agree. Likelihood tolerance is absolute 1e-6 plus relative 1e-8; inference uses absolute 2e-5 plus relative 2e-3; estimates use absolute 2e-5 plus relative 2e-4. Group modes use absolute 5e-5 because large-sample flat-profile optimization produced shifts around 2e-5 in modes near zero; relative error there is not informative. These tolerances apply to phit against R. The SciPy reference is checked against R as a peer, with group modes at absolute 2e-4, because its independent optimizer stops at a slightly different point on the same flat profile.
The installed lme4 version disables derivative checks automatically at large n. The benchmark explicitly enables the final joint Hessian. Its initial BOBYQA run also stopped short on the 10,000-row case; an R-only restart from that fit, with rhobeg=0.001 and nAGQ0initStep=FALSE, resolved it. Both R stages are included in its fit time. The report records these controls, versions and data/binary hashes. Native estimates never seed the R worker.

title: Probit regression scale validation and performance
text:
Simulation and agreement
Study hours are uniform between 1 and 12. Practice scores are 45 + 3 × hours plus normal noise with standard deviation 8, clipped. The wider case adds independent standard-normal extra scores. Outcomes are draws from
\[\pi_i=\Phi(-1.9+0.13\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.011\,\mathrm{score}_i
+0.08\sum_j\mathrm{extra}_{ij}),\qquad y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).\]
This simulation is separate from the small teaching sample. Data hashes, generating coefficients, and sample correlations are recorded.
Coefficient-level quantities and scalar statistics are compared with R at 1e-9 + 1e-7 * abs(reference). Fitted values and residuals are computed in full and compared at ten evenly spaced rows; the small fixtures compare full vectors. phit must report convergence within 1 to 100 updates. Wald intervals follow R confint.default(), and the null baseline follows the documented intercept convention. Probit covariance uses expected Fisher information in all three runtimes.

Reproduction

QUARTO_PYTHON="$PWD/.context/notebooks-venv/bin/python" \

Set matching PHP and PHP_CONFIG, and use .so on Linux. For a quick check that leaves the published report unchanged, add --cases 1000:3 --repeats 2 --output .context/probit-smoke.json. A numerical failure aborts the run without writing results.

title: API overview
text:
The extension registers the PHP module phit (extension=phit, Composer ext-phit). Every function is in the Phit namespace and is named by prefix. The polyfill defines the same functions except the CSV reader; see Extension or polyfill.
Import the functions you use:
stubs/phit.php in the repository declares every signature with PHPDoc array shapes for IDEs and static analysis. Do not load it at runtime.

title: API overview
text:
Deprecated aliases
fit_lm, fit_glm, fit_lmer, fit_glmer, fit_logistic, fit_probit, fit_poisson, fit_mixed, fit_mixed_intercept, and fit_logistic_mixed, and fit_ols called with a matrix, still exist as deprecated aliases: each call raises E_USER_DEPRECATED that names the current function and returns its result.

title: API overview
text:
Signatures
The formula functions are listed in Model formulas. The four fixed-effect matrix functions share one signature:
// fit_ols_matrix, fit_logistic_matrix,
// fit_probit_matrix, fit_poisson_matrix
Phit\fit_ols_matrix(
    array $x,
    array $y,
    string $missing = 'drop',
    ?array $weights = null,
    ?array $offset = null,
    bool $intercept = true,
): array;
Matrix model functions lists the mixed-model matrix signatures.
Every estimator is synchronous and stateless:

It returns a complete fit and keeps no model handle, input data, or configuration.
It does not modify the caller’s arrays.
Repeated fits are independent.

title: API overview
text:
Formula interfaces
The formula functions build R’s model.matrix() over named columns and fit it with the estimator of the matching matrix function. Each result has that matrix function’s complete contract plus naming keys (formula, response, columns, terms, assign, intercept, named, predvars, and, for fit_generalized_linear and fit_mixed_logistic, family and link).







Failure
Code




Unknown column, malformed factor descriptor, referenced list-column, or invalid formula
1001


Columns of different lengths
1002


Infinite transform result
1003


Rank-deficient design
1004


Unsupported function, family, link, or random-effect structure
1007



Model formulas defines the syntax, data shapes, contrasts, missing-value handling, and differences from R.

title: API overview
text:
Matrix model contracts
Matrix model functions defines the inputs, results, convergence rules, and failure cases of each matrix function:

OLS
Binary logistic regression
Probit regression
Poisson regression
Gaussian random-intercept mixed model
Weights, offsets and grouped binomial responses
General Gaussian mixed model
Binomial random-intercept model

title: API overview
text:
Fixed intercept
The seven matrix functions take bool $intercept = true.

With the default, supply predictor columns only. phit prepends an exact ones column, and the intercept is coefficient 0, followed by the predictors in column order. Covariance, standard errors, tests, and intervals follow the same order.
Parameter counts and residual degrees of freedom include the added coefficient.
intercept: false uses x exactly. Use it for a model through the origin, or for a design that already contains a ones column.
phit does not detect existing constant columns. Leaving a ones column in x with the default creates a duplicate intercept and raises a rank-deficiency error.
For an intercept-only fit, supply one empty predictor row per outcome, such as x: array_fill(0, count($y), []). Empty predictor rows require intercept: true.
Random-effect designs (random[*].z) are not affected. A random intercept and slope still needs [1, slope] rows.

title: API overview
text:
Input conversion

Numeric elements must be PHP integers or floats. Values are not coerced from strings.
PHP integers are converted to 64-bit floats, so integers beyond 2^53 can lose precision.
Arrays are read in iteration order, and keys are ignored. Row order aligns x with y, and column order aligns every coefficient result. Keep labels separately.
null and NAN are missing. By default, rows with missing values are deleted with one E_WARNING, and missing: 'raise' rejects them. fitted and residuals follow retained_rows. See Missing values.
phit does not add columns or remove aliased predictors.
Arithmetic is 64-bit floating point. Extreme input scales can exceed its range.

title: API overview
text:
Diagnostics and error codes

Exceptions
Statistical and input failures throw a PHP Exception with a numeric getCode():








Code
Category
Meaning




1001
Invalid input
Type, domain, or control error; missing: 'raise'; invalid groups, weights, or counts


1002
Dimension mismatch
Shape or alignment error, or too few residual observations


1003
Nonfinite
Nonfinite values, or arithmetic beyond floating-point range, including nonzero residual variance that underflows


1004
Rank deficiency
Numerical rank failure of the design or information


1005
Factorization failure
A required linear solve or positive-definite factorization fails


1006
Nonconvergence
Iteration budget, line search, optimizer, or score failure; separation; an optimum at a search boundary


1007
Unsupported
An explicit size or count limit, or an unimplemented configuration


1008
Internal
A required decomposition output is missing, or an internal invariant fails




There are no estimator-specific exception classes. Handle Throwable at the application boundary, since PHP argument and runtime errors use their own types.
Message text can change. Use the code, not the message.
When several checks fail, the exception can report the first, or the most relevant category.
Invalid data are checked before missing-value deletion.
Zend TypeError, result-conversion errors, and caught Rust panics are runtime errors, not statistical codes.
If neither the extension nor the polyfill is loaded, the functions do not exist. That is an installation failure.



Diagnostics
Every successful estimator returns diagnostics:







Key
Contents




converged
true on every returned fit, including direct OLS. A failed fit throws.


solver
scaled_svd, newton_irls, fisher_scoring, profile_variance_search, bobyqa, or nelder_mead


iterations, evaluations
Present when the result has the top-level key of the same name, with the same value


gradient_max
Binomial mixed model only; the same value as its top-level key


boundary, singular
Present when the estimator reports that flag. A zero variance is a valid fit.


warnings
list<string>: missing-row deletion, a near-singular covariance, or the binomial mixed model’s Laplace advisory




The warnings are interpretation notices. Only missing-row deletion also raises a PHP E_WARNING.
Diagnostics that do not apply are omitted. phit does not invent an iteration count or a gradient.
General Gaussian mixed fits check optimizer termination, parameter bounds, valid factors, and finite output. They have no final gradient or Hessian check on the variance parameters.
Wald inference and local convergence do not establish model adequacy or quadrature accuracy.



Undefined values and limits

NAN and INF in a successful result are values, not failure markers. An exact zero-residual OLS fit keeps its documented NAN and INF statistics, while nonzero variance that underflows raises 1003.
PHP’s json_encode() with JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR rejects NAN and INF, so JSON consumers must handle them explicitly.
Binomial models allow at most 1,000,000 trials per original row. Accepted success counts are rounded with round(y*trials)/trials.

title: API overview
text:
Implementation notes
The Rust core takes the design literally and has no PHP dependency:
pub fn fit_ols(
    x: Vec<Vec<f64>>,
    y: Vec<f64>,
) -> Result<OlsResult, StatsError>

OlsResult has the statistical fields of the PHP array, with Vec<f64> for lists, Vec<Vec<f64>> for covariance, Vec<[f64; 2]> for confidence intervals, f64 for scalars, and usize for residual degrees of freedom. Missing-value deletion and its metadata exist only in the PHP binding.
StatsError::new(kind, message) carries an explicit ErrorKind. kind() returns the category, and .0 the message. The binding maps each ErrorKind to the codes above.
The binding converts values and errors. It does not implement statistical formulas.

See Design philosophy for the boundary between this API and optional convenience layers.

title: Deploying to servers
text: The deployed PHP process needs only phit.so and its system libraries. Rust, Clang, PIE, R and Python are build or development tools and are not needed at runtime. Installation covers PIE and the prebuilt binaries; this page covers PHP-FPM, containers and manual builds.

title: Deploying to servers
text:
Names

Composer and PIE package: phpstats/phit.
Registered extension: phit. Use it with extension_loaded('phit'), phpversion('phit'), get_extension_funcs('phit') and Composer’s ext-phit.
Installed module: phit.so. A direct Cargo build produces libphit.so on Linux and libphit.dylib on macOS; they are the same extension.
Functions are in the Phit namespace, such as Phit\fit_ols.

title: Deploying to servers
text:
Supported targets
The extension supports PHP 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5, non-thread-safe, on Linux and macOS. Windows and ZTS builds are not supported. The prebuilt binaries, which pie install downloads on Linux, are built on Debian Bookworm for x86_64 and arm64 and need glibc 2.35 or later. Alpine (musl) and older glibc releases need a source build with PIE or by hand. CI tests Linux x86_64 and arm64 at all three PHP versions, and macOS on Apple silicon.

title: Deploying to servers
text:
PHP-FPM
PHP loads the extension when a process starts. After installing or replacing phit.so:

Enable it in the configuration PHP-FPM reads. php --ini shows the CLI’s files, which can differ from FPM’s.
Restart the PHP-FPM service so every worker loads the new module.
Check the web runtime, not only the CLI, for example with extension_loaded('phit') and phpversion('phit') in a request.

Each call does its work within the request. There is no background process, subprocess, or network service.

title: Deploying to servers
text:
A PHP-FPM container image
docker/Dockerfile builds a PHP-FPM image with the extension installed. From the repository root:
docker build --target checks -f docker/Dockerfile -t phit:checks .
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t phit:local .
./scripts/check-container phit:local phit:checks

The build installs the extension with PIE 1.5.0 and runs the Rust and PHP checks.
check-container sends a FastCGI request to an isolated FPM container, then runs the production image’s CLI and FPM with its shipped PHP configuration. Both must give identical OLS coefficients and a Poisson fit with a log-exposure offset.
The final image holds the PHP runtime and the extension. Rust, Clang, PIE, Python, sources, and test tools stay in the build stages.
The image keeps the official PHP entrypoint and runs PHP-FPM in the foreground.

Use it as an application base:
FROM phit:local
COPY app/ /var/www/html/
Connect your web server to FPM, which speaks FastCGI rather than HTTP.

Build pins and reproducibility







Input
Pinned by




PHP and Rust base images
OCI digest, one PHP digest each for 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5; build and runtime stages share the PHP image


Rust dependencies
Cargo.lock


PIE PHAR
SHA-256


Debian APT packages
Not pinned; resolved at build time



Update the pins deliberately and rerun the checks. Because APT packages are not pinned, a rebuild is repeatable but not byte-identical. Binary manifests record the compiler, PHP API, architecture, libc, linked libraries, extension hash, and Cargo.lock hash.

title: Deploying to servers
text:
Manual build without PIE
From a checkout of the repository or the release’s source archive, the standard phpize build works without PIE. pie/config.m4 and pie/Makefile.frag run the locked Cargo build:
cd pie
/path/to/phpize
./configure --with-php-config=/path/to/php-config
make -j4
# Stage without modifying the installed PHP runtime:
make install INSTALL_ROOT=/absolute/path/to/staging
# Or install after reviewing the build:
# sudo make install

Build as an unprivileged user. make install needs the built module and does not rerun Cargo under sudo.
INSTALL_ROOT stages under the configured extension directory.
On macOS, use the LLVM and header setup in the development guide.
After installing, add extension=phit.so to the PHP configuration. Check php --ini for the CLI and the FPM configuration separately, and confirm the functions load in both.
Rebuild for another PHP ABI, architecture, thread-safety or debug configuration, or platform.

title: Design philosophy
text: phit provides statistical models and numerical routines through PHP functions with explicit inputs and array results. Numerical behavior is checked against reference implementations on shared inputs.

title: Design philosophy
text:
Principles

Plain inputs and outputs. Functions take PHP arrays, or a table object with toModelData() or toColumns(), and return associative arrays. There are no model objects or services.
Two levels of input. The formula functions build a design from named columns as R does. The *_matrix functions take a literal design for code that builds its own. Both call the same estimators.
Documented defaults. OLS inference is homoskedastic with 95% t intervals. Logistic, probit, and Poisson fits use maximum likelihood with 95% normal Wald intervals. Rank-deficient designs are rejected, and undefined statistics are NAN or INF.
Visible missing-data handling. Incomplete rows are dropped with a warning and reported in every result, or rejected with missing: 'raise'. See Missing values.
Evidence for each estimator. Each estimator has a mathematical walkthrough and a comparison with R, lme4, or statsmodels where they support it. Agreement is claimed only for the tested cases.
Simple implementation. Each model has a dedicated estimator. phit has no general GLM framework and no generic Model, Family, Link, or Optimizer traits for hypothetical future models.

title: Design philosophy
text:
Architecture







Component
Responsibility




stats-core
Estimation, inference, and numerical validation. It takes Rust vectors and returns a dedicated result struct or a StatsError, with no PHP types.


php-extension
PHP value inspection, formula parsing and design construction, numeric conversion, missing-row filtering with warnings and accounting, exceptions, result arrays, and the CSV reader.


Rust crates
Matrix decompositions, special functions, and optimizers. phit’s own code expresses the statistical formulas.



phit uses Rust-native numerical crates. An external BLAS or LAPACK backend needs a demonstrated numerical, performance, or deployment benefit and must preserve the contract and reference agreement.

title: Design philosophy
text:
Scope
phit fits OLS, binomial logistic and probit regression, Poisson regression, Gaussian mixed models by ML or REML with random intercepts and slopes, and a binomial logistic model with one random intercept by Laplace or adaptive quadrature. It also provides probability distributions, descriptive statistics, seeded sampling, posterior-draw kernels, and a CSV reader. The R compatibility ledger lists what is supported, what differs, and what is not supported.
The posterior-draw functions are numerical kernels for CmdStanPHP’s moment matching: weighted moments, covariance maps, and affine transforms. They use literal row and parameter order, never insert an intercept, and never drop rows. Stan evaluation, PSIS, iteration control, and diagnostics belong to the consuming package. See Posterior draws.
Before a feature is added, decide whether it changes estimation or only prepares data:

Data preparation belongs in packages such as phibble and phpolars, or in application code.
A numerical feature needs a concrete use case, an explicit contract, and verification before it enters the engine.
A new dependency or abstraction must solve a demonstrated problem.

title: Design philosophy
text:
Data preparation
phit reads CSV files and builds designs from formulas. Other preparation, such as selecting records, converting text under an explicit policy, or attaching labels, belongs to the caller or to table packages. Preparation code should make its choices visible: column order, intercept insertion, missing-value handling, and row alignment. It should preserve phit’s result or document any transformation, such as replacing nonfinite values for JSON.

title: Design philosophy
text:
Conventions for documentation and evidence
These conventions apply to contributors writing walkthroughs, verifications, and benchmarks.

Teaching data. Main examples use reproducible simulations with named variables, units, plausible ranges, and noise. Pages label the data as simulated, state the generating equation and seed, and save the observations so that Rust, PHP, R, and statsmodels fit the same sample. They report observed correlations rather than the intended relationship.
Walkthroughs. They distinguish observed inputs, constructed columns such as the intercept, generating parameters, trial values, and estimates. Matrix dimensions and intermediate values appear beside the steps. Small samples keep matrices readable, and their statistical limits are stated.
Shared samples. docs/data/housing.csv comes from tests/generate-learning-data.R, and docs/data/learning.csv from tests/generate-logistic-fixtures.R.
Benchmarks. Each estimator with reference support has an API-level benchmark against R and statsmodels. Numerical agreement on identical inputs is checked before timings are published. Reports record versions, machine, threads, raw measurements, and timing boundaries, and separate fitting from startup. Benchmarks are development commands, not unit tests.
Mixed models. Gaussian mixed models keep the marginal likelihood, variance components, and conditional group estimates visible in the code. BOBYQA and Nelder–Mead come from pinned Rust crates. The NLopt and PORT backends that lme4 can use are not available.
Approximate likelihoods. For non-Gaussian mixed models, pages separate agreement with R from integration accuracy. They state the approximation, compare like methods, and check node-count sensitivity with an independent integrator.

title: Probability distributions
text: Evaluate densities, probabilities, and quantiles for 12 distribution families in 13 parameterizations (negative binomial has two), one value at a time or for a whole array. Each function returns a PHP float or a packed PHP array.

Families and parameters
Each row is one parameterization. Parameters are listed in call order, with defaults. Every parameter must be finite and inside its domain.

Gamma’s second parameter is a scale. Exponential’s is a rate.
Negative-binomial size is a positive real dispersion parameter, not a trial count. The two forms agree when prob = size / (size + mu).
Poisson lambda = 0, binomial size = 0 or prob of 0 or 1, and negative-binomial prob = 1 or mu = 0 are point masses.

title: Probability distributions
text:
Batch evaluation

The output is a packed list in input iteration order. Keys are not kept.
Empty input returns [], but the parameters are still validated.
One invalid element rejects the whole call. No elements are dropped.
The distribution is constructed once per call. The benchmarks show when batching saves PHP call overhead.

title: Probability distributions
Probability distributions
text:
Boundaries

Outside the support, a density or mass is 0 and its log is -INF.
A boundary density can be infinite, for example a beta density with a shape below one at an endpoint.
A discrete PMF at a non-integer count is 0. CDF and SF use the floor of the evaluation point, and SF always means strictly greater.
Continuous quantiles at p = 0 and p = 1 are the support bounds, including infinities.
A discrete quantile is the smallest support value whose CDF reaches p. The comparison allows a relative 64 * EPSILON on the smaller tail, to absorb rounding at CDF steps. A point mass returns its location at p = 1, which differs from R and SciPy in some degenerate cases.
Count quantiles are returned as PHP floats, so they are exact only up to 2^53.

title: Probability distributions
text:
Errors







Input
Result

Evaluated at the limit


Evaluation point NAN
Exception 1003

null, numeric string, boolean, or nested array in a batch

Exception 1006



Scalar argument types follow PHP’s usual rules. There is no missing option. The last row covers a beta-type sum a + b beyond the double range, a beta-type parameter above 10^300 evaluated within 10^-300 of a support endpoint, and a gamma-type shape or point above 10^300. Examples are dist_f_cdf(2, 3, PHP_FLOAT_MAX) and dist_gamma_cdf(1e30, 1e30).

title: Probability distributions
text:
Evidence

Distributions: verification compares phit with R, SciPy, and 60-digit mpmath references, with tolerances for each quantity and the documented boundary differences.
Distributions: performance covers 1,000, 100,000, and one million values, including peak memory.

title: Probability distributions
text:
Implementation notes
The distribution functions use their own module, not the estimators’ statrs paths. An audit of statrs 0.19 on the saved R cases (raw results) found lost small tails, a relative binomial CDF error near 4.8e-4 at size one million, and inaccurate extreme quantiles. statrs has no log-tail API, so the audit used log(CDF) and log(SF).

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Compute weighted moments of a draw matrix, a map between two covariance matrices, and an affine transformation of the draws with its log Jacobian. The kernels support PSIS-LOO moment matching in a PHP CmdStan interface, and they work on any numeric matrix with draws in rows.
The caller owns model evaluation, importance ratios, PSIS, iteration control, and diagnostics. The kernels add no fitting, plotting, or model objects.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Weighted moments
For \(X\in\mathbb R^{S\times P}\), nonnegative weights are normalized to \(w_i\) with \(\sum_i w_i=1\). weights: null gives \(w_i=1/S\).
\[
\mu=\sum_i w_i x_i,\qquad
C_{\mathrm{pop}}=\sum_i w_i(x_i-\mu)(x_i-\mu)^T,\qquad
C_{\mathrm{unbiased}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{pop}}}{1-\sum_i w_i^2}.
\]

unbiased uses reliability weights, not frequency counts. Multiplying all weights by a positive constant does not change the result.
Uniform weights give divisor S for the population covariance and S − 1 for the unbiased covariance.
A singular covariance is a valid moment result.
Zero-weight rows contribute nothing but are still validated.
The unbiased denominator \(1-\sum_i w_i^2\) is computed in binary64. A zero or negative value is rejected, including weights so concentrated that they round to one effective draw. No other effective-sample-size cutoff applies.

Numerical method: weights are divided by their maximum before compensated summation, so weights whose ordinary sum would overflow still work. The mean uses an anchor from a positive-weight draw, a compensated sum of deviations, and a second correction pass. The covariance uses compensated centered cross-products and is returned exactly symmetric. Together these avoid cancellation from a large common offset.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Covariance map
With lower Cholesky factors \(C_s=L_sL_s^T\) and \(C_t=L_tL_t^T\), the map solves
\[
L_s^T A^T=L_t^T,\qquad A C_s A^T=C_t.
\]

No inverse is formed.
The log Jacobian is \(\sum_j\log (L_{t,jj})-\log(L_{s,jj})\), so a very large or small determinant need not be representable.
The map depends on parameter order and is one of many covariance maps.

Both covariances must pass a numerical check before factorization. Let \(d_i=\sqrt{C_{ii}}\) and \(R_{ij}=C_{ij}/d_i/d_j\).

Each diagonal must be strictly positive.
Opposite standardized entries a and b must satisfy \(|a-b|\le64\epsilon\max(1,|a|,|b|)\), with \(\epsilon=2^{-52}\). Accepted asymmetry is averaged on this scale.
R must have a Cholesky factor, and each squared diagonal pivot must exceed \(64\epsilon P\). The factor’s rows are then rescaled by \(d_i\).

These checks do not depend on the units of individual parameters. They define a pivot threshold, not a condition-number guarantee, and near the threshold rounding and parameter order can decide acceptance. No jitter, ridge, eigenvalue clipping, or fallback factorization is applied. A singular covariance that draws_moments() returns is therefore rejected by draws_covariance_map().

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Affine transformation
Each draw, as a column vector, becomes \(y_i=A x_i+b\). With draws in rows, the implementation computes \(Y=X A^T+\mathbf1 b^T\). No intercept column is added, and draw order is kept.
Invertibility is checked on an equilibrated matrix. Each row of A is divided by its largest absolute element, then each column of the result by its largest absolute element. A zero row or column is singular. The equilibrated matrix B must satisfy
\[
\sigma_{\min}(B)>64\epsilon P\sigma_{\max}(B).
\]

SVD assesses numerical rank, and pivoted LU supplies the log absolute pivots.
The log determinant adds the logs of the row and column scales. Summing logs avoids overflow and underflow, and absolute pivots allow reflections and negative determinants.
Scales are applied by division, which handles subnormal values.
A numerically singular matrix raises 1004.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Limits
All arithmetic is binary64. Finite inputs can still produce nonfinite intermediate or final values at extreme scales, which raises 1003 rather than returning NAN or INF. Relative accuracy is not guaranteed for underflow-sized covariances or arbitrarily ill-conditioned inputs.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Independent verification
tests/generate-draw-fixtures.py produces 25 cases with Python’s standard-library Decimal at 80 digits. It uses scalar loops for the weighted formulas, a scalar Cholesky and backward solve, and pivoted Gauss–Jordan elimination for reference inverses and log determinants. It never calls the extension or nalgebra.







Quantity
Tolerance




All fixture outputs (Rust and PHP)
\(10^{-11}+10^{-11}\lvert\mathrm{reference}\rvert\)


Extreme-scale nonzero affine outputs, covariance identities
Also relative \(10^{-12}\)


Affine round trips, forward plus reverse log determinants
\(10^{-11}+10^{-11}\lvert\mathrm{reference}\rvert\)



The cases cover correlated parameters, uniform, nonuniform, and zero weights, weight rescaling, one effective draw, singular covariance, one parameter, large offsets, mixed units, orientation, reflections, determinant overflow and underflow, invalid arrays, and the thresholds. Rust also checks the weighted covariance transformation under both normalizations. PHP checks named arguments, defaults, iteration order, and strict rejection without missing-row warnings.
tests/fixtures/draws-python.json records the Python version, algorithm, and tolerances, and the provenance manifest hashes the generator and fixture. The regular tests need neither R nor Python.
# Refresh the reference deliberately.
python3 tests/generate-draw-fixtures.py
python3 scripts/reference-manifest.py
cargo test -p stats-core --locked --test draws

PHP=/path/to/php PHP_CONFIG=/path/to/php-config ./scripts/check

title: Fit a mixed model
text:
Interpretation

(1 | school) gives each school its own intercept, assumed to come from a normal distribution. The fit uses REML, as lme4::lmer() does by default.
The study_hours coefficient is an association within schools. The model gives every school the same slope.
The school SD describes how school intercepts vary. The residual SD describes how students vary around their school’s line.
With six schools, the school SD is estimated imprecisely.
effects are each school’s predicted intercept relative to the average, as R’s ranef() reports. They are shrunk toward zero, more so for schools with fewer students.
The conditional standard errors are equal because every school has five students.

See also: Mixed models for the supported structures, the full result, singular fits, and fit_mixed_logistic() · Interactive shrinkage vignette

title: Extension or polyfill
text: phit has two implementations of the Phit\ functions. Code written against one runs unchanged on the other, unless it reads CSV files through phit.

title: Extension or polyfill
text:
Versions
Each polyfill release reproduces one phit release. Polyfill 0.4.2 reproduces phit v0.4.4 and provides 242 of its 243 functions, including the deprecated aliases.

title: Extension or polyfill
text:
How they coexist

Composer loads the polyfill’s bootstrap.php through its files autoload. If extension_loaded('phit') is true, the bootstrap defines nothing, so every Phit\ function is the extension’s. Installing both is safe.
The polyfill does not fill gaps in an older extension. If the loaded extension is older than the polyfill’s phit release, functions added since then stay undefined.
The polyfill’s composer.json declares "provide": {"ext-phit": "*"}, so it satisfies a package that requires ext-phit, including one that uses the CSV reader.
Without the extension, function_exists('Phit\read_csv') and class_exists('Phit\CsvReader') return false, as does Phit\Polyfill::supports('Phit\read_csv'). phibble’s DataFrame::fromCsv() then uses its own PHP reader.

title: Extension or polyfill
text:
Differences

The listwise-deletion warning is E_USER_WARNING in the polyfill and E_WARNING in the extension. The text is the same.
Arguments of the wrong scalar type follow PHP’s userland rules in the polyfill: coercion, or a TypeError under strict_types.
Every polyfill function throws an exception with code 1007 while OPcache’s JIT compiles the process, because the JIT has produced wrong numerical results in the polyfill. The JIT is off by default in PHP 8.4 and 8.5, and PHP 8.3’s defaults (opcache.jit=tracing with opcache.jit_buffer_size=0) also leave it off.
On an x86-64 CPU without fused multiply-add, the extension’s products of matrices larger than 5×5 can differ from the polyfill’s in the last bit.

title: Installation
text:
Install phit with PIE:
phit is a PHP extension, so it is installed once per PHP installation rather than per Composer project. Projects that cannot install extensions can use the polyfill, which provides every function except the CSV reader.

text:
Requirements



Requirement
Supported




PHP
8.3, 8.4, and 8.5, non-thread-safe (NTS) builds. Thread-safe (ZTS) builds are not supported.


Operating system
Linux and macOS. Windows is not supported.

title: Installation
text:
How PIE installs phit
PIE finds the latest release on Packagist, installs phit.so into the extension directory, and enables it for the PHP it runs under. To target another PHP installation, pass --with-php-config=/path/to/php-config.

Linux x86_64 and arm64 with glibc 2.35 or later: PIE downloads a prebuilt binary. No compiler or Rust toolchain is needed.
macOS, Alpine and other musl systems, and glibc older than 2.35: PIE builds from source. See Building from source.

title: Installation
text:
Building from source
The build needs these tools, which are not needed at runtime:

phpize and php-config from the same PHP installation
a C toolchain with autoconf and make
stable Rust from rustup
Clang and libclang

On Debian or Ubuntu:
sudo apt-get install build-essential autoconf pkg-config \
  clang libclang-dev php-dev
curl -fsSL https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
In the official php:*-cli images, PHP’s development files are present. Add Clang, libclang, and the image’s $PHPIZE_DEPS.
On macOS, install the Xcode command-line tools (xcode-select --install), Rust from rustup, and PHP and autoconf from Homebrew (brew install php autoconf). If the build cannot find libclang, the development guide shows the variables that select Homebrew’s LLVM.

title: Mixed models
text: fit_mixed_gaussian() fits Gaussian linear mixed models, as lme4::lmer() does. fit_mixed_logistic() fits a binomial logit model with one random intercept, as lme4::glmer() does for that structure. It fits no other family or link, so it has no family or link arguments. Both take an R formula with lme4’s bar syntax for random effects.

title: Mixed models
text:
Supported structures









Function
Random terms
Family and link
Fitting method




fit_mixed_gaussian
(1 | g), (x | g), (0 + x | g), (x || g) (uncorrelated), several terms such as (1 | g1) + (1 | g2), interaction groups (1 | g1:g2), and nesting (1 | g1/g2)
Gaussian, identity
REML (default) or ML (reml: false); BOBYQA (default) or Nelder–Mead (optimizer: 'nelder_mead')


fit_mixed_logistic
Exactly one (1 | g)
Binomial, logit
ML by Laplace (quadraturePoints: 1, the default) or adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature with 2 to 61 points



Any other random-effect structure, family or link throws code 1007. Random slopes, several random terms, the Poisson and probit families, and REML are not available in fit_mixed_logistic(). Random-effect terms in fit_ols() or fit_generalized_linear() also throw code 1007.

The term’s k×k random-effect covariance

One row of conditional modes per group

One k×k conditional covariance per group, lme4’s ranef(condVar = TRUE)

Groups in order of first appearance after missing-value deletion




lme4 sorts groups instead. The estimates do not depend on the order.
The fixed-effect tests use the normal distribution. lme4 reports t values without p-values, and packages such as lmerTest add degrees-of-freedom approximations. phit has no degrees-of-freedom correction.
With few groups, Wald inference for the fixed effects can be optimistic.

title: Mixed models
text:
Singular fits
A random-effect variance estimated at or near zero, or a correlation at ±1, makes the covariance singular. The fit returns with singular true and the warning random-effect covariance is singular or near singular in diagnostics.warnings. With these data, score ~ study_hours + (1 + study_hours | school) is singular because the estimated slope variance is near zero. A singular fit usually means the random-effect structure is more complex than the data support.

title: Mixed models
text:
A binomial random-intercept model
docs/data/cbpp.csv holds lme4’s cbpp data: cases of contagious bovine pleuropneumonia in 15 herds over four periods.
use function Phit\{fit_mixed_logistic, read_csv};

$csv = read_csv(
    'docs/data/cbpp.csv',
    ['types' => ['c', 'i', 'i', 'c']],
);
$herds = array_combine(
    $csv['names'],
    array_column($csv['columns'], 'values'),
);
$herds['healthy'] = array_map(
    fn ($n, $k) => $n - $k,
    $herds['size'],
    $herds['incidence'],
);

$fit = fit_mixed_logistic(
    'cbind(incidence, healthy) ~ period + (1 | herd)',
    $herds,
    quadraturePoints: 10,
);
foreach ($fit['named'] as $name => $b) {
    printf("%-12s %8.4f\n", $name, $b);
}
printf(
    "herd SD %.4f, %s\n",
    $fit['random_intercept_sd'],
    $fit['integration'],
);
(Intercept)   -1.3992
period2       -0.9914
period3       -1.1278
period4       -1.5795
herd SD 0.6475, adaptive_gauss_hermite

quadraturePoints is lme4’s nAGQ. The Laplace default (1) is fastest.
More points approximate the likelihood more closely, which matters most for small groups and rare events.
No number of points guarantees accuracy for every data set. Compare a few values when the estimates matter.
A row may have at most 1,000,000 trials, counted as cbind() successes plus failures or as weights. Larger counts throw an exception with code 1007.

A fit_mixed_logistic result has the fixed-effect keys of fit_mixed_gaussian and these:







Key
Contents




random_effects, random_effects_cond_var
Each group’s conditional mode (log-odds scale) and its conditional variance


group_labels, group_sizes, n_groups
Groups in order of first appearance


random_intercept_variance, random_intercept_sd
The estimated group variance and SD


linear_predictor
Log odds at the conditional modes


neg2_log_likelihood
−2 × the approximate marginal log-likelihood


quadrature_points, integration
The node count and laplace or adaptive_gauss_hermite


gradient_max, boundary
Largest absolute score at the optimum; whether the group variance is exactly zero

title: Mixed models
text:
Prediction

predict() adds each known group’s random effects by default, as lme4’s re.form = NULL does.
random: false predicts at the population level, and the grouping columns can then be absent.
A group the fit never saw throws code 1001 unless allowNewLevels: true, which predicts it at the population level.
Mixed-model predictions have no standard errors, as in lme4.

R seed 20261015 generates 250 students in 12 schools with different group sizes. Study hours are uniform from 1 to 12; prior scores are clipped 40 + 3 × hours + normal noise with standard deviation 8, then rounded. Assessment scores follow

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
text:
2. Conditional and marginal models
The conditional model is
\[y\mid b\sim N(X\beta+Zb,\sigma^2 I),\qquad b\sim N(0,\tau^2 I_G).\]
Fixed effects beta describe the population relationship. Random intercepts b are modeled as draws from a common zero-mean distribution, not G freely estimated fixed coefficients. sigma² is within-school residual variance; tau² is between-school variance after accounting for X. Normality and independence are modeling assumptions.
Marginalizing over b gives
\[y\sim N(X\beta,V),\qquad V=\sigma^2 I+\tau^2 ZZ^\top.\]
For two different students in the same school, covariance is tau². For different schools it is zero. A single student’s marginal residual variance is sigma² + tau². The intraclass correlation, conditional on fixed predictors, is
\[\mathrm{ICC}=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}.\]
This is not the raw Pearson correlation of the observed scores. The covariance structure concerns unexplained variation after accounting for fixed effects. For a school of size m,
\[V_g=\sigma^2 I_m+\tau^2\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top.\]

# Display a block using generating variances, not fitted or starting parameters.
m=len(members[0]);Vg=25*np.eye(m)+36*np.ones((m,m))
show_matrix(r'V_{\mathrm{school\ 1}}\text{ at generating parameters}',Vg)
print('Generating ICC:',36/(36+25))

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
section: 3. The likelihood integrates out group effects
text:
3. The likelihood integrates out group effects
The marginal Gaussian log-likelihood is
\[\ell(\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)=-\frac12\left[
n\log(2\pi)+\log|V|+(y-X\beta)^\top V^{-1}(y-X\beta)\right].\]
This is not a Gaussian likelihood using conditional residuals as independent observations, and not the joint likelihood obtained by treating b as ordinary fixed parameters. It includes the covariance determinant and integrates over b.
For fixed variance components, maximizing over beta gives generalized least squares (GLS):
\[X^\top V^{-1}X\hat\beta=X^\top V^{-1}y.\]
OLS assumes covariance proportional to I. GLS changes how residual directions are weighted because group means and within-group deviations have different variances. The production solve uses whitening and SVD, rather than inverting this cross-product.

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
section: 4. Whiten groups instead of building a huge matrix
text:
4. Whiten groups instead of building a huge matrix
Write rho=tau²/sigma² and C=I+rho ZZ’. For one group,
\[C_g=I_m+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top,\quad
C_g^{-1}=I_m-\frac{\rho}{1+m\rho}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top,\quad
\log|C_g|=\log(1+m\rho).\]
The group-mean direction has eigenvalue 1+m rho; all m-1 directions orthogonal to it have eigenvalue 1. Whitening preserves within-group deviations and divides the mean by sqrt(1+m rho):
\[C_g^{-1/2}v=(v-\bar v\mathbf1)+\frac{\bar v}{\sqrt{1+m\rho}}\mathbf1.\]
This transformation applies to y and each column of X. The squared whitened residual norm is q=(y-X beta)’ C^-1 (y-X beta). It requires storage linear in n, without constructing the full n × n V. Scaling X’s columns as D gives A=XD^-1; weighted SVD solves C^-1/2 A theta approximately C^-1/2 y, with beta=D^-1 theta.

scales=np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0);A=X/scales

def whiten(values,rho):
    matrix=np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim==1:matrix=matrix[:,None]
    output=matrix.copy()
    for indices in members:
        mean=matrix[indices].mean(axis=0)
        output[indices]=(matrix[indices]-mean)+mean/np.sqrt(1+len(indices)*rho)
    return output

rho_trial=1.0
show_matrix(r'C_{g}^{-1}\text{ at trial }\rho=1',np.eye(m)-np.ones((m,m))/(1+m))
show_matrix(r'C^{-1/2}X\text{ at trial }\rho=1',whiten(X,rho_trial))
show_matrix(r'C^{-1/2}y\text{ at trial }\rho=1',whiten(y,rho_trial))
wx=whiten(X,rho_trial);wy=whiten(y,rho_trial)[:,0]
show_dot(r'(X^\top C^{-1}y)_2',wx[:,1],wy)
show_matrix(r'X^\top C^{-1}X\text{ for illustration}',wx.T@wx)

Trial rho is a starting/example variance ratio, not an observed predictor or a known generating parameter. The cross-product shown is for understanding the dot products; production estimation uses the SVD of an equivalent compact weighted design, derived next.

Cache a square-root reduction, following the lme4 idea
lme4 evaluates a penalized least-squares problem and eliminates the random coefficients through a block factorization. For our single random intercept, the same elimination has a particularly simple form. At positive rho,
\[\min_b\left\{\sum_{i\in g}(r_i-b)^2+\frac{b^2}{\rho}\right\}
=\sum_{i\in g}(r_i-\bar r_g)^2+\frac{m_g\bar r_g^2}{1+m_g\rho}.\]
The minimizer is \(b=m_g\rho\bar r_g/(1+m_g\rho)\); substitute it into the left side to obtain the right side. At rho=0 the limiting solution has b=0. Within-group deviations have weight 1; only the group-mean weight changes with the variance ratio. This is the link between penalized least squares and the marginal GLS residual norm above.
We can therefore do most observation-level work once. Let W contain within-group-centered rows of the augmented matrix \([A\;y]\), and let row g of M be \(\sqrt{m_g}[\bar A_g\;\bar y_g]\). Take a thin QR factorization \(W=Q_wR_w\). Since \(Q_w^\top Q_w=I\), for any coefficient vector theta,
\[q(\rho,\theta)=\left\|W\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2
+\sum_g\frac{\left(M_g\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right)^2}{1+m_g\rho}
=\left\|K(\rho)\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2,\]
\[K(\rho)=\begin{bmatrix}R_w\\
\operatorname{diag}\{(1+m_g\rho)^{-1/2}\}M\end{bmatrix}.\]
K has only p+1+G rows. The fixed intercept’s centered column is zero; that poses no problem for QR of the augmented matrix. Full rank is checked on the complete weighted fixed design, including the group-mean rows.

augmented=np.column_stack([A,y])
centered=augmented.copy();means=[];sizes=np.array([len(rows) for rows in members])
for rows in members:
    mean=augmented[rows].mean(axis=0)
    centered[rows]=augmented[rows]-mean
    means.append(np.sqrt(len(rows))*mean)
means=np.asarray(means)
_,within_R=np.linalg.qr(centered,mode='reduced')
compact=np.vstack([within_R,means/np.sqrt(1+sizes[:,None]*rho_trial)])
show_matrix(r'R_w',within_R)
show_matrix(r'K(\rho=1)',compact)
trial_theta=np.array([40.,1.,.1])*scales
contrast=np.r_[-trial_theta,1.]
compressed_q=np.linalg.norm(compact@contrast)**2
full_q=np.linalg.norm(whiten(y-X@(trial_theta/scales),rho_trial))**2
np.testing.assert_allclose(compressed_q,full_q,atol=1e-8,rtol=1e-12)

phit caches R_w and M once, then uses SVD on the compact weighted fixed design. Covariance is computed only at the selected fit. The later Python profile deliberately uses the full whitening formulation as an independent check of the same mathematics. For a million observations and 100 groups with three coefficients, each trial factors 104 rows instead of a million.
This borrows elimination and reuse from lme4; it does not copy lme4 source code or introduce its sparse Cholesky/CHOLMOD backend. Using QR/SVD square roots also avoids subtracting nearly equal Gram matrices or forming a residual norm as \(y^\top y-\hat\beta^\top X^\top y\). That preserves accuracy with correlated predictors and small residual variation. See lme4’s PLS versus GLS derivation and the measured optimization.

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
section: 5. Profile out beta and sigma²; optimize one variance ratio
text:
5. Profile out beta and sigma²; optimize one variance ratio
At fixed rho, GLS finds beta and q. The ML scale estimate is
\[\hat\sigma^2(\rho)=q(\rho)/n,\qquad\hat\tau^2=\rho\hat\sigma^2.\]
Substitution gives the profiled negative log-likelihood
\[f(\rho)=\frac12\left[n\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/n)\}
+\sum_g\log(1+m_g\rho)\right].\]
A lower value is better. No generic multivariate optimizer is required for this particular random-intercept model. For GLS residuals r=y-X beta, the envelope theorem lets us differentiate the optimized objective without differentiating beta:
\[q'(\rho)=-\sum_g\frac{(\sum_{i\in g}r_i)^2}{(1+m_g\rho)^2},\qquad
f'(\rho)=\frac12\left[n\frac{q'}q+\sum_g\frac{m_g}{1+m_g\rho}\right].\]
Rust searches t=log(1+rho) on a 0.5-spaced grid from 0 to 32, then refines every negative-to-positive derivative crossing by 40 bisections. The derivative with respect to t is (1+rho)f’(rho). It compares those candidates with rho=0 exactly, and rejects an optimum beyond the upper bound. The finite grid can miss unusually narrow unbracketed stationary points: this initial search is not an exhaustive global-optimum guarantee. The Python walkthrough independently brackets roots of the same score, using SciPy’s root solver.

def profile(t):
    rho=np.expm1(t);wx=whiten(A,rho);wy=whiten(y,rho)[:,0]
    U,s,Vt=np.linalg.svd(wx,full_matrices=False)
    beta=(Vt.T@((U.T@wy)/s))/scales
    residual=y-X@beta
    q=np.sum(whiten(residual,rho)**2);variance=q/n
    logdet=sum(np.log1p(len(indices)*rho) for indices in members)
    objective=.5*(n*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1+np.log(variance))+logdet)
    qprime=-sum((residual[indices].sum()/(1+len(indices)*rho))**2 for indices in members)
    derivative=.5*(1+rho)*(n*qprime/q+sum(len(indices)/(1+len(indices)*rho) for indices in members))
    return dict(rho=rho,beta=beta,variance=variance,objective=objective,derivative=derivative,s=s,Vt=Vt)

grid=np.arange(0,32.5,.5);values=[profile(t) for t in grid];candidates=[0.]
for left,right,a,b in zip(grid[:-1],grid[1:],values[:-1],values[1:]):
    if a['derivative']<0 and b['derivative']>=0:
        candidates.append(brentq(lambda t:profile(t)['derivative'],left,right,xtol=1e-12))
best_t=min(candidates,key=lambda t:profile(t)['objective'])
fit=profile(best_t);rho=fit['rho'];beta=fit['beta'];variance=fit['variance'];tau=rho*variance
print('Candidate log ratios:',candidates)
print('Residual variance:',variance,'Group variance:',tau,'ICC:',rho/(1+rho))
show_matrix(r'\hat\beta',beta)

curve=np.linspace(0,4,81);objective=np.array([profile(t)['objective'] for t in curve])
render_figure('profile',dict(curve=curve.tolist(),objective=(objective-objective.min()).tolist(),
                           best_t=float(best_t),boundary=float(profile(0)['objective']-objective.min())))

ML is not REML. Restricted maximum likelihood adjusts for estimating fixed coefficients and adds a fixed-design determinant term; it often improves variance estimation with limited groups. R lmer defaults to REML, so all comparisons here explicitly set REML=FALSE. No RSS/(n-p) correction is substituted for the ML scale.

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
text:
6. Shrinkage: estimate each school’s intercept
At the fitted variances, the Gaussian conditional mean of a group effect is
\[\hat b_g=\frac{m_g\hat\tau^2}{\hat\sigma^2+m_g\hat\tau^2}\bar r_g,
\qquad\bar r_g=\frac1{m_g}\sum_{i\in g}(y_i-x_i^\top\hat\beta).\]
To derive it, combine the prior term b²/tau² with the within-group likelihood sum(r_i-b)²/sigma². The resulting quadratic in b has precision 1/tau² + m/sigma² and linear term sum r_i/sigma², yielding this conditional mean. The multiplier lies between 0 and 1: noisy/small groups shrink more toward zero. These empirical BLUPs use fitted variances; they are not known realized effects. At tau²=0 all group effects are zero.

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
text:
7. Fixed-effect uncertainty and model statistics
The plug-in GLS covariance is
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat V^{-1}X)^{-1}
=\hat\sigma^2 D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1},\]
where V and S on the right are the SVD factors of the whitened scaled design (the SVD factor V is distinct from the observation covariance V). Standard errors are diagonal square roots. We report asymptotic normal Wald z-tests and intervals. There is no exact OLS t distribution, Satterthwaite/Kenward–Roger adjustment or variance-component p-value. With only twelve groups, normal inference should be read cautiously: many students do not substitute for many independent groups.
AIC uses p+2 parameters: fixed coefficients and both variance components, counting them even when tau²=0. Group BLUPs are not counted as G additional free parameters. The returned df_residual=n-p is informational, not a t-test denominator.

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
text:
8. Boundaries, assumptions and experiments
A zero random-intercept variance is a valid boundary ML fit. It gives OLS fixed coefficients but uses the ML scale RSS/n for standard errors, rather than OLS’s unbiased RSS/(n-p). Positive residual variance is required; numerically perfect fits and unsupported zero-residual-variance limits fail. One group or all-singleton data are rejected because the two variances cannot be separately identified under this first contract; singleton groups are allowed when other groups repeat.
Assumptions include independent groups, Gaussian random intercepts independent of X, homoskedastic Gaussian residuals and the supplied linear fixed mean. Ignoring correlation between random effects and predictors can bias fixed effects. The first implementation has one grouping factor, no random slopes or REML. Missing rows in x, y or groups are deleted together, with warnings and row metadata.
Try merging all groups into one; assigning each row a new group; removing the school variation in the simulation; or increasing residual noise. Which makes the model unidentified, pushes group variance to zero, or increases shrinkage?

title: Gaussian mixed models: covariance, marginal likelihood and shrinkage
text:
Rust connections
fit_random_intercept owns numeric vectors and usize group IDs. A HashMap assigns first-appearance group indices; vectors of member row positions make group means and group means explicit. ProfileData caches a QR square-root summary and group means; a private Profile struct holds one variance-ratio evaluation. nalgebra’s SVD handles compact GLS and final covariance; the dedicated scalar search remains visible in crates/stats-core/src/mixed.rs. Result/? propagates validation and numerical errors. The binding preserves typed PHP group labels, handles missing rows and converts the complete result to ordinary arrays.
See the PHP contract, executed comparison, lme4 lmer reference, and statsmodels MixedLM.

title: The same random-intercept ML model in R, Python and PHP
text:
Conventions that must match
ML is explicit: R and statsmodels otherwise support/default to REML, which fits a different variance criterion. Likelihood here integrates over group effects. Fixed-effect standard errors use plug-in GLS covariance (X’ V^-1 X)^-1, matching lme4. statsmodels’ reported joint observed-Hessian covariance can differ, so the Python runner explicitly recalculates the declared GLS convention using its fitted variance components; it does not claim its unmodified bse_fe matches every case. Normal z-based Wald intervals are constructed explicitly for every reference.
Our df_residual=n-p is informational. R mixed-model df methods may include the two variance parameters; no finite-sample t degrees of freedom are claimed here. AIC counts p+2 parameters in every case, including a zero variance boundary.
The exact tau²=0 fixture is checked against lme4 and PHP, with a separately labeled NumPy OLS-limit reference. It is not represented as a converged statsmodels mixed fit. At this boundary, variance is RSS/n and standard errors differ from OLS’s unbiased-scale inference. This explicit check avoids treating an approximate positive-variance optimizer solution as proof of exact boundary behavior.

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text: This walkthrough models a binary or grouped-binomial outcome with a Gaussian random intercept. The outcome distribution changes; the group-effect distribution remains Gaussian. This walkthrough uses the published cattle-disease cbpp data from lme4, with 56 herd/period records across 15 herds. Period one is the baseline. Data source: Lesnoff et al. (2004), Preventive Veterinary Medicine 64, 27–40. The CSV, provenance/checksum and license are included in the site.

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text:
Observed counts and constructed predictors
\[
s_i\mid b_{g(i)}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m_i,p_i),\qquad
\eta_i=o_i+x_i^\top\beta+b_{g(i)},\qquad p_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}.
\]
Here s is the observed number of new cases and m the number of animals at risk. The API takes y=s/m and weights=m; m=1 gives ordinary binary observations. The known offset o is zero in this example. The fixed columns are ones and indicators for observed periods 2, 3 and 4. These are data/prepared predictors, not guesses at coefficients.

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text:
Conditional likelihood and random-effect law
For one observation,
\[
\log f(s_i\mid b)=\log {m_i\choose s_i}
+s_i\eta_i-m_i\log(1+e^{\eta_i}).
\]
We specify b_g~N(0,tau²). Write b_g=tau*u_g with u_g~N(0,1), so zero tau is a valid boundary without computing log(0). The fixed coefficients and tau are estimated by marginal maximum likelihood:
\[
L(\beta,\tau)=\prod_g\int
\left\{\prod_{i\in g}f(s_i\mid u_g;\beta,\tau)\right\}
\phi(u_g)\,du_g.
\]
We integrate over unobserved group effects. Merely finding their best values and ignoring this integral would fit a different objective. No prior is placed on beta or tau in this implementation; the Gaussian distribution describes population variation among groups.

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text:
Find each conditional mode
Apart from constants independent of u, the log integrand is
\[
k_g(u)=\sum_{i\in g}\{s_i\eta_i-m_i\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\}-\tfrac12u^2.
\]
Its score and negative curvature are
\[
k'_g(u)=\tau\sum_{i\in g}(s_i-m_ip_i)-u,\qquad
h_g(u)=-k''_g(u)=1+\tau^2\sum_{i\in g}m_ip_i(1-p_i).
\]
The prior contributes the 1, making the log integrand strictly concave: every group has a unique conditional mode, even when all its outcomes are failures or successes. Safeguarded Newton updates use u + score/h; a bracket prevents an oversized step from escaping the root.

e=x[ids]@beta;yg=y[ids];mg=m[ids]
def kernel(u):
    eta=e+tau*u
    return -.5*u*u-np.sum(mg*(yg*np.logaddexp(0,-eta)+(1-yg)*np.logaddexp(0,eta)))
mode=brentq(lambda u:tau*np.sum(mg*(yg-expit(e+tau*u)))-u,-20,20,xtol=1e-13)
p=expit(e+tau*mode);h=1+tau*tau*np.sum(mg*p*(1-p))
display(pd.DataFrame(dict(period=raw.iloc[ids].period,successes=s[ids],trials=mg,
                         fixed_log_odds=e,conditional_log_odds=e+tau*mode,
                         probability=p,score_contribution=s[ids]-mg*p,
                         information_contribution=mg*p*(1-p))))
print('Conditional standardized mode:',mode)
print('Random intercept b=tau*u:',tau*mode)
print('Score at mode:',tau*np.sum(mg*(yg-p))-mode)
print('Posterior precision:',h)

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
section: Laplace approximation: use height and curvature
text:
Laplace approximation: use height and curvature
Approximating k by a quadratic near its mode gives
\[
\log L_g\approx\sum_{i\in g}\log{m_i\choose s_i}
+k_g(\hat u_g)-\tfrac12\log h_g.
\]
The Gaussian prior’s normalization cancels the quadratic integral’s sqrt(2*pi). The curvature term is essential: a narrow peak has less probability mass than a wide peak of the same height. This is the default one-node approximation, matching lme4 glmer(nAGQ=1).

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text:
Adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature
Let z_j,w_j integrate expectations under N(0,1). Center and scale those nodes at the conditional mode: u_j=mode+z_j/sqrt(h). Then
\[
L_g\approx\left\{\prod_{i\in g}{m_i\choose s_i}\right\}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_g}}\sum_jw_j
\exp\{k_g(u_j)+z_j^2/2\}.
\]

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
section: Fixed-effect uncertainty comes from the marginal objective
text:
Fixed-effect uncertainty comes from the marginal objective
The optimizer searches beta and tau jointly. Each objective evaluation solves all conditional modes and integrates the group effects. Fixed-effect covariance uses the beta block of the inverse joint observed information of the chosen approximate marginal likelihood. It includes coupling to estimated tau; it is not simply the inverse conditional X’WX matrix.

likelihood=evaluator(c);theta=np.r_[beta,tau]
def information(step):
    delta=step*(1+abs(theta));n=len(theta);H=np.zeros((n,n))
    objective=lambda t:-likelihood(t[:-1],t[-1],61)[0]
    f0=objective(theta)
    for i in range(n):
        a=theta.copy();b=theta.copy();a[i]+=delta[i];b[i]-=delta[i]
        H[i,i]=(objective(a)+objective(b)-2*f0)/delta[i]**2
        for j in range(i):
            pp=theta.copy();pm=theta.copy();mp=theta.copy();mm=theta.copy()
            pp[i]+=delta[i];pp[j]+=delta[j];pm[i]+=delta[i];pm[j]-=delta[j]
            mp[i]-=delta[i];mp[j]+=delta[j];mm[i]-=delta[i];mm[j]-=delta[j]
            H[i,j]=H[j,i]=(objective(pp)-objective(pm)-objective(mp)+objective(mm))/(4*delta[i]*delta[j])
    return H
H=(4*information(5e-4)-information(1e-3))/3
cov=cho_solve(cho_factor(H),np.eye(len(theta)))[:-1,:-1]
matrix(H,r'H_{\beta,\tau}')
matrix(cov,r'\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)')
print('Standard errors:',np.sqrt(cov.diagonal()))
assert np.allclose(cov,fit['covariance'],atol=1e-6,rtol=1e-4)

Standard errors: [0.23351159 0.30676799 0.32676837 0.4275945 ]


The implementation uses centered finite differences with Richardson extrapolation, then a Cholesky solve. Nonpositive information, nonstationary solutions and exhausted optimizer budgets fail explicitly. Standard errors, z tests and 95% normal Wald intervals are asymptotic approximations. There are no random-variance intervals, finite-group t corrections or REML in this binomial fitter.

title: Binomial mixed models: likelihood, latent effects and integration
text:
Approximation accuracy: a rare-event example
The verification includes independent QUADPACK integration, which does not use Hermite nodes. On the rare-event sample, Laplace and R agree but the fitted group SD differs substantially from higher-node estimation. This is an approximation issue, not a disagreement between implementations.

rare=[r for r in report['results'] if r['dataset']=='rare_events']
display(pd.DataFrame([dict(nodes=r['quadrature_points'],intercept=r['PHP']['coefficients'][0],
                          group_SD=r['PHP']['random_intercept_sd'],
                          approximate_log_likelihood=r['PHP']['log_likelihood'],
                          independently_integrated_log_likelihood=r['scipy_integrated_log_likelihood'],
                          approximation_error=r['approximation_log_likelihood_error']) for r in rare]))
# Compare posterior shape with the Gaussian approximation in a small group.
rc=next(c for c in fixture['cases'] if c['name']=='rare_events_61')
rf=next(r['PHP'] for r in rare if r['quadrature_points']==61)
rx=np.array(rc['x']);ry=np.array(rc['y']);rg=np.array(rc['groups']);rtau=rf['random_intercept_sd'];re=rx@np.array(rf['coefficients'])
choices=[]
for group in dict.fromkeys(rg):
    ids=rg==group;ee=re[ids];yy=ry[ids]
    k=lambda u,ee=ee,yy=yy:-.5*u*u-np.sum(yy*np.logaddexp(0,-ee-rtau*u)+(1-yy)*np.logaddexp(0,ee+rtau*u))
    uu=brentq(lambda u:rtau*np.sum(yy-expit(ee+rtau*u))-u,-30,30)
    hh=1+rtau*rtau*np.sum(expit(ee+rtau*uu)*expit(-ee-rtau*uu))
    norm=quad(lambda u:np.exp(k(u)-k(uu)),-np.inf,np.inf,epsabs=1e-11)[0]
    error=k(uu)-.5*np.log(hh)-(k(uu)+np.log(norm)-.5*np.log(2*np.pi))
    choices.append((abs(error),group,k,uu,hh,norm))
_,group,k,uu,hh,norm=max(choices,key=lambda v:v[0])
u=np.linspace(-4,4,400)
actual=np.array([np.exp(k(v)-k(uu))/norm for v in u]);gaussian=np.sqrt(hh/(2*np.pi))*np.exp(-.5*hh*(u-uu)**2)
render_figure('posterior',dict(u=u.tolist(),actual=actual.tolist(),gaussian=gaussian.tolist(),

title: OLS verification: R, statsmodels and PHP
text:
Limits
The harness excludes perfect and zero fits from three-way finite comparisons: floating-point residuals can differ dramatically relative to their tiny magnitudes, and some inference is undefined. The Rust/PHP test suites cover those conventions separately. phit rejects singular designs, so they are not compared with references that alias coefficients.
The tolerance includes an absolute floor; it does not promise relative accuracy for extremely small p-values. This notebook verifies these cases in the recorded environment, not every dataset or platform. See Verification for coverage and fixture maintenance.
Sources: R lm, statsmodels OLS, statsmodels missing-data behavior.
